# Registration log (public copy)

This is the registration log of the work reported in "How Many Atoms, Where, and When". It lists, in order of time, the
predictions that were fixed before the quantities they predict were computed, the results of those computations, the tests that
failed or could not be decided, and the corrections.

How to read an entry. Each entry starts with a line of the form "## Amendment N (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM) - title". Times are those of
the computer clock, UTC+07:00. Where the original entry recorded a date without a time, only the date is given. An entry marked
PRE-REGISTERED states a prediction, its acceptance band and the script that reads the outcome, before the outcome existed. An
entry marked RESULT gives the outcome of an earlier registration and the verdict of its script. Failed and void tests stay in the
log with their verdicts. A correction is a new entry that names the entry it corrects; earlier entries are not rewritten.

Limits. The log was kept in this repository and was not deposited with an independent registry, so its dates rest on the record of
the repository.

What this copy leaves out. It omits notes on private correspondence and on the arrangements of the work. It also omits sentences
about the preparation of the manuscripts, such as editing passes and checks of wording, numbers and citations, about software
tooling, and about maintenance of the computer. An entry whose whole content was of that kind keeps its header and the line
"Content omitted: preparation of the manuscript." The first person singular of the original is written as "we". No prediction,
acceptance band, result or verdict was changed. REDACTIONS.md lists every entry that differs from the original and the kind of
change. The original log is kept by the author.

# PRE-REGISTRATION — Q32: an UPPER bound on the support size, by counting zeros of the KKT function
Written 2026-09-04 21:20, before any new computation, after the lower-bound route was closed (see
Q31_PROOF.md section F and WALL_ANALYSIS.md).

## Why this target and not the other two
The published bracket is Omega(sqrt A) below and O(A) above (Dytso, Barletta, Shamai 2021; Dytso et al. 2024).
Our certified counts sit at 0.89 sqrt(A) + 1.08, so the truth is near the LOWER end and the upper bound is the
loose side, off by a factor of order sqrt(A). Improving O(A) to O(sqrt(A) polylog A) would therefore be a real
narrowing of a stated open problem, and it is the side our evidence supports rather than the side it merely
fails to contradict.
The alternative lane, promoting the Poisson-Gaussian correspondence to a theorem, is weaker on our own data:
the measured differences N_Gauss - N_Poisson at A = 25, 50, 100, 150, 200, 300, 400, 500 are 0, 1, 1, 3, 3, 1,
2, 3, which we cannot presently distinguish from slow growth, so we would be trying to prove boundedness that
our numbers do not clearly show. Recorded so the choice is auditable.

## The object
Let Q* be the capacity-achieving output and D(x) = KL(Poisson(x) || Q*). The KKT conditions say D(x) <= C on
[0, A] with equality exactly on the support. Since D is real-analytic on (0, infinity) and D - C <= 0, every
support point is a zero of D - C, and every interior support point is a DOUBLE zero (the function touches zero
from below, so D'(x) = 0 there as well). Hence
    N*(A) <= 1 + (number of zeros of D - C in [0, A]) and in fact 2 N*(A) - 2 <= (number counted with multiplicity).
An upper bound on the zero count is an upper bound on the support size. This route never mentions a reference
prior, which is what blocked the lower-bound route.

## Predictions, fixed now
- P-sqrt: the zero count of D - C in [0, A] is at most c sqrt(A) log^p A for some constants c and p >= 0. Then
  N*(A) = O(sqrt(A) polylog A), improving the published O(A).
- P-linear: the best available growth estimate yields only O(A), i.e. the analytic-function route cannot beat
  the published bound without new structure. Then say exactly which estimate is the obstruction.
- P-partial: an intermediate bound such as O(A^{3/4}) or O(sqrt(A) exp(c sqrt(log A))). Report it as such.

## Falsifiers from our own data (any proof must respect these)
1. The count is at least 0.89 sqrt(A), so no upper bound below that can be correct.
2. Consecutive zeros are spaced about 2.2 sqrt(x) apart, so a proof implying spacing that is asymptotically
   larger or smaller by a growing factor contradicts measurement.
3. D - C is not small between support points: we will measure its depth between consecutive zeros and record it
   here as Amendment 1 before the proof attempt starts, since any zero-counting argument depends on how deep the dips
   are and a proof asserting a different depth is wrong.

## Method
Measure the dip depths and the local behaviour of D - C on our certified optima first, so the proof attempt works
against numbers rather than intuition. Then make one proof attempt under the corrected discipline: output to a named
file, every constant checked numerically, every premise labelled as measured, standard or
assumed. An independent check of every load-bearing inequality before anything is recorded.

## Amendment 1 (2026-09-04 21:25) - the dips are tiny, and our instrument cannot see them at large A
Note in the original header: Measured before the proof attempt starts.
Depth of C - D(x) at its minimum between consecutive support points (`q32_dips_log.txt`):
| A | N | min / median / max depth | depth x sqrt(x), median |
|---|---|---|---|
| 50 | 7 | 3.0e-4 / 2.7e-3 / 1.7e-1 | 0.0086 |
| 100 | 10 | -5.0e-9 / 2.5e-4 / 1.7e-1 | 0.0009 |
| 200 | 14 | -1.6e-5 / 1.0e-4 / 1.7e-1 | 0.0009 |
| 500 | 21 | -1.0e-4 / 7.6e-5 / 1.7e-1 | 0.0009 |
| 1000 | 29 | -2.6e-7 / -2.5e-7 / 1.7e-1 | -0.0000 |
Three facts, and one of them is a limit on us.
1. The largest dip, about 0.17, is always the first gap, near the silent end; everywhere else the function hugs
   its maximum to within 1e-4 or less. So D - C is extremely flat across most of [0, A].
2. The depth falls faster than 1/sqrt(x): the product drops by a factor ten from A = 50 to A = 100 and then sits
   near 0.0009, which is itself suspicious.
3. NEGATIVE depths appear at A = 100 and above, meaning D exceeds C between support points, which violates the
   KKT condition. That is not a property of the channel; it is our solver's residual, which we already recorded
   as 3e-5 to 2e-3 above A = 75. So the dip measurement is BELOW OUR INSTRUMENT'S PRECISION for A >= 100 and is
   only trustworthy at A = 50, where the median depth is 2.7e-3.
CONSEQUENCE for the route. A zero-counting argument needs to know how far D - C stays below zero between its
zeros, because that is what separates genuine zeros from near-degenerate ones. Our numbers say the separation is
minute and we cannot currently measure it where it matters. So this lane carries an instrument requirement
before it carries a proof: a higher-precision solver (extended precision, or the KKT system solved in exact
rational arithmetic at small A) to measure the dip law. That requirement is recorded now so the proof attempt is not
asked to prove something about a quantity we have not measured.

## Amendment 2 (2026-09-04 21:35) - the extended-precision measurement, and it overturns Amendment 1
Built `support_mp.py`: mpmath at 30 digits, the exact KKT system solved by Newton with a numerical Jacobian.
Newton residuals: 9.9e-21 at A = 20, 1.5e-17 at A = 50, 3.0e-10 at A = 100 (the last not yet converged).
Dip depths of C - D between consecutive support points:
| A | median | min | max | all positive? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20 | 3.09e-5 | 6.25e-6 | 7.45e-5 | yes |
| 50 | 5.18e-6 | 1.28e-6 | 7.01e-5 | yes |
| 100 | 2.83e-7 | -2.59e-5 | 6.28e-5 | no (not converged) |
Two corrections to Amendment 1, both in the same direction: the dips are POSITIVE everywhere once the optimum
is solved properly, so the negative values were solver error as suspected; and they are far SMALLER than the
double-precision numbers suggested (median 5.2e-6 at A = 50 against the 2.7e-3 reported before, a factor of
520). The earlier figure was measuring our own residual.
Measured law, and its uncertainty, stated honestly: from the two trustworthy rows the exponent is between
-1.5 and -2.0 depending on which median convention is used for the even-length list at A = 20 (medians 1.94e-5
or 3.09e-5), giving -1.54 or -1.95. TWO POINTS CANNOT PIN AN EXPONENT. A third converged amplitude is required
before any exponent is quoted, and A = 100 is running at higher precision for that purpose. Until then the only
safe statement is that the depth is of order 1e-5 to 1e-6 in this range and falls faster than 1/A.
CONSEQUENCE for the route, stated before any proof attempt. The KKT function sits within about 1e-5 to 1e-6 of
its maximum across the whole interval apart from the first gap, at these amplitudes. Any zero-counting argument must therefore work at
that scale: a perturbation or growth estimate that is only accurate to A^{-1} cannot distinguish the zeros at
all. This is a sharp and useful constraint for the proof attempt, and it is the kind of quantity that would
have been invented rather than measured if we had gone straight to the mathematics.

## Amendment 3 (2026-09-04 21:45) - BOTH counting criteria were wrong, in opposite directions
The extended-precision solve at A = 100 reached a Newton residual of 8.45e-25, so the KKT system is solved
exactly, and yet max_x D(x) - C = +2.588e-05 at x = 26.4455. A converged solution of the stationarity system
that violates D <= C is not the optimum. Decisive test: we added an atom at that point and re-optimised, from
both the double-precision and the extended-precision solutions. Capacity rose from 1.759639706245 to
1.759640288260 and 1.759640298927, a gain of 5.8e-7 and 5.9e-7. So N*(100) >= 11, and our reported 10 is WRONG.
Diagnosis of both criteria:
- The slack criterion (solver v3) OVER-counts: it keeps adding atoms because its slack never reaches the
  tolerance, the extra atoms carrying negligible weight.
- The degeneracy criterion (solver v6) UNDER-counts: when the optimiser fails to find the better solution at
  K + 1, a weight collapses to the bound and the criterion reads that as saturation. That is what happened at
  A = 100, where the K = 11 optimisation in the sweep missed a solution worth 5.9e-7 more.
- The gold standard is the KKT slack itself, since D(x) <= C is necessary AND sufficient, but it must be
  compared against the numerical floor of the slack computation, which is about 3e-8 at A = 20 and grows with A.
  At A = 100 the violation is 2.6e-5, three orders above that floor, so it is real.
Corrected procedure, now running (`q32_ktest.py`): for each K, multi-start optimisation, then report capacity
AND slack; N* is the smallest K whose slack sits at the floor. First result: at A = 20 the answer is 5, with
slack 3.0e-8 at K = 5 and no capacity gain for any larger K, so that row stands.
CONSEQUENCE: the staircase in PREREG_Q30 Amendment 9, and everything fitted to it (the 0.89 sqrt(A) + 1.08 law,
the spacing constant 2.2, the gap x N law), must be recomputed with the corrected procedure before any of it is
quoted again. Marked in the audit package as provisional.

## Amendment 4 (2026-09-04 22:05) - the count is only measurable up to about A = 50 with double precision
Built `support_cp.py`, a cutting plane whose new atom is placed AT THE ARGMAX of D and whose start is the
current optimum. That warm start finds solutions the cold multi-start misses, which was the whole cause of the
under-count. Results:
| A | N* (this method) | previous v6 | capacity |
|---|---|---|---|
| 20 | 5 | 5 | 1.142117421749 |
| 50 | 7 | 7 | 1.479921347185 |
| 100 | 16, raw 18 | 10 | 1.759640322988 |
At A = 20 and 50 the answer is stable and the weights are all of order 0.1, so those rows are solid. At A = 100
the method keeps finding capacity gains: 1.7596397062 at ten atoms, 1.7596402989 at eleven, 1.7596403230 by
eighteen, with the last atoms carrying weights of 3.6e-4 and 1.7e-9. The gains after the eleventh atom total
2.4e-8, which is at the level where double-precision mutual information is no longer trustworthy.
HONEST CONCLUSION, and it is a bigger correction than Amendment 3. The capacity is extraordinarily flat in the
number of atoms: past a certain point, extra atoms buy gains of 1e-8 and smaller, and whether they belong to the
true optimal support cannot be decided in double precision. Our counting is therefore reliable only up to about
A = 50 with the present tools. Everything reported for A >= 100, in either direction, is an artefact of where a
particular optimiser stopped. The staircase above A = 50 is WITHDRAWN pending an extended-precision optimiser
(not merely an extended-precision polish), and with it the fitted count law, the spacing constant, the
correspondence table and the gap law, all of which were fitted mostly on amplitudes above 50.
What survives untouched: the lower-bound route's closure (Q31), which rests on Theorem E and on the gap law's
SHAPE rather than its fitted constant, and the two rows at A = 20 and 50.

## Amendment 5 (2026-09-04 22:25) - the hybrid counter, and the error has a direction
Pure mpmath cutting plane failed (Newton alone diverges from a warm start: at A = 20 it returned 1.0961 at
K = 4 against the true 1.1421). The working architecture is HYBRID: double precision finds the K-atom
configuration by SLSQP, mpmath at 30 digits decides whether the extra atom really gains capacity
(`q32_hybrid.py`).
| A | v3 (slack) | v6 (degeneracy) | cutting plane, double | hybrid, mp-decided | sqrt(A) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 4.47 |
| 50 | 7 | 7 | 7 | 7 | 7.07 |
| 75 | 9 | 9 | - | 10 | 8.66 |
| 100 | 11 | 10 | 16 | 14 | 10.00 |
THE ERROR HAS A DIRECTION, and it matters more than any single number: every improvement of the instrument has
RAISED the count. The hybrid ratios N/sqrt(A) are 1.12, 0.99, 1.15, 1.40 at A = 20, 50, 75, 100, rising rather
than flat. Our earlier conclusion, that the data favour sqrt(A) over sqrt(A log A), was drawn from counts we now
know were low, and a rising ratio is what a logarithmic factor looks like.
NOT decisive, and we will not claim it is. The A = 100 hybrid value is itself a lower bound: the procedure
stopped because the double-precision optimiser returned a degenerate weight at K = 15 while the mp capacity was
still gaining 4.0e-9. So the honest statement is that N*(100) >= 14, that all our counts above A = 50 are lower
bounds, and that the direction of every correction so far has been upward.

## Amendment 6 (2026-09-04 22:15) - the count at A = 100 is 11, and our chain of corrections went in a circle
The build-up methods over-count because the double-precision optimiser's error (about 1e-9 in capacity) is
larger than the capacity difference between neighbouring K. The decisive instrument is to build up and then
MERGE DOWN, re-optimising at each step, and take the K where the mp capacity peaks with all weights healthy.
At A = 100 (`q32_overcount_test_log.txt`):
| K | 17 | 16 | 15 | 14 | 13 | 12 | 11 | 10 | 9 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| mp capacity | ...32414 | ...32445 | ...32447 | ...32428 | ...32468 | ...32478 | **...32483** | ...970619 | ...7364 |
| smallest weight | 1.1e-8 | 1.6e-14 | 6.9e-9 | 2.8e-14 | 1.1e-14 | 2.3e-4 | **3.3e-2** | 7.8e-2 | 9.6e-2 |
Capacity peaks at K = 11, where every weight is healthy; K = 12 and above do not improve it and carry atoms of
weight 1e-14, while K = 10 is worse by 6e-7. So N*(100) = 11.
THE FULL SEQUENCE OF OUR ANSWERS AT A = 100, IN ORDER: 11 (slack criterion), 10 (degeneracy criterion), 14
(hybrid), 16 and 18 (cutting plane and corrected hybrid), 11 (merge-down). The first answer was right, and I
spent a day travelling away from it and back. Every intermediate step was an instrument artefact, and each time
We recorded the new number as a correction of the old one with an argument that read convincingly.
What this costs: Amendment 5's claim that "the error has a direction and every improvement raises the count" is
WITHDRAWN. The direction was upward only while the build-up procedures were dominant; the merge-down test
reverses it. So the reading that our data may favour a logarithmic factor after all is also withdrawn, and we
are back to the position that the range A <= 100 is consistent with about 1 + sqrt(A).
What survives, and is now better founded: the counting procedure itself. Build up past the peak, merge down with
re-optimisation, and take the peak of the mp capacity with healthy weights. That is the instrument the staircase
must be recomputed with.

## Amendment 9 (2026-09-04 23:20) - A = 100 settled as far as it can be, and the threshold is honoured
Merging the eighteen-atom solution down to eleven and re-optimising gives a solution with all weights healthy
(smallest 3.26e-2), the highest capacity anyone has found at this amplitude (1.75964032488659), and an mp slack
of 1.0897e-7. The certificate floor at the settled amplitudes was 1.2e-8 to 3.8e-8, and our pre-set threshold for
"certified" was 1e-7. The value misses it by a factor of about three, so by the rule fixed in advance,
A = 100 IS NOT CERTIFIED, and we record it as the best candidate rather than as an answer.
Two readings, both stated: the slack floor grows with amplitude across the settled points, so a floor near 1e-7
at A = 100 is plausible and the eleven-atom answer is probably right; and the threshold was set in advance
precisely so that "probably right" does not become "reported as measured".
FINAL STATE OF THE STAIRCASE: certified at A = 20, 30, 50, 75 with N* = 5, 6, 7, 9; best candidate 11 at
A = 100 without a certificate; nothing above that. The figure has been rebuilt to show exactly this.

## Amendment 10 (2026-09-04 23:35) - A = 100 is undetermined between eleven and twelve, and that is the final word
Floor-versus-count test at A = 100: starting from the eleven-atom solution (slack 1.0897e-7, argmax at
x = 43.50), adding an atom there and re-optimising gives a twelve-atom solution with capacity CHANGE
-1.88e-10, i.e. no gain, weights still healthy (smallest 5.74e-3), and slack 5.53e-8.
Reading, with both sides stated. The capacity is identical between eleven and twelve atoms to two parts in
ten billion, so capacity cannot separate them. The slack halves, from 1.09e-7 to 5.53e-8, and the floor
measured at the settled amplitudes runs from 1.2e-8 to 8.7e-8, so the twelve-atom value sits inside that band
while the eleven-atom value sits just above it. By the rule we fixed in advance (a factor of three) the change
counts as "at the floor", but the halving is a real signal and we are not going to bury it.
CONCLUSION: A = 100 is undetermined between N* = 11 and N* = 12 with our tools. Neither is certified. The
staircase therefore ends at A = 75, exactly as the plan anticipated, and no further amplitude will
be attempted until the instrument improves. This is the closing state of Q32's measurement phase.

## Amendment 11 (2026-09-05 00:30) - the slack is not monotone in K, so last night's halving carries no information
Test (`q32_spurious_slack.py`). At the four certified amplitudes, take every configuration with K > N*, where the
extra atoms are known to be spurious because their weights sit at the 1e-14 floor, and compare the KKT slack
there with the slack at N*.
RESULT: of 14 such rows, the slack falls BELOW its certified value in 7, with ratios down to 0.102. The slack is
not monotone in K and a smaller slack at K+1 is not evidence that K+1 atoms are needed.
CONSEQUENCE FOR A = 100. The observed drop from 1.0897e-7 at eleven atoms to 5.5263e-8 at twelve is a ratio of
0.507, comfortably inside the range that certainly-spurious atoms produce. Amendment 10 treated that halving as
a real signal to be weighed against the capacity. It is not a signal. The capacity change was already negative,
so the only remaining anomaly at A = 100 is that the twelfth weight did not collapse to the 1e-14 floor as it
does at every certified amplitude. That single anomaly is now being tested directly against the exact KKT system
at 40 digits (`q32_A100_newton.py`), which asks whether a twelve-atom KKT point with healthy weights exists at all.

## Amendment 12 (2026-09-05 00:20) - an accidental import destroyed three of the four certified amplitudes
`q32_slack2.py` has no main guard, so importing it from another script re-ran the entire sweep and began

Method rule this produces: a script that writes a result file in place must refuse to be imported, and any

## Amendment 13 (2026-09-05 00:50) - the instrument was broken in a way that explains every failure at A = 100
The exact-KKT test at A = 100 returned INCONCLUSIVE: Newton reached only 5.98e-6 at eleven atoms, made the
slack worse (1.09e-7 -> 6.10e-6), and diverged outright at twelve (residual 1.316, capacity collapsing to 1.55).
That contradicted the record, which had the same solver converging at A = 100 to 8.45e-25. Checking the stored
solution showed why: that converged run had TEN atoms, not eleven. A converged solution of the stationarity
system at fixed K is the best K-atom input, not the channel optimum; ten atoms have a large positive slack and
are certainly not enough, and eleven beat ten by 6.19e-7, far above the 1e-9 noise, so N*(100) >= 11 is settled.
DIAGNOSIS of the failure, and it is not the flatness of D. `support_mp.solve` computes D'(x) by a central
difference with h = 1e-13, then builds the Jacobian by differencing that with dh = 1e-20. The position block
holds D''(x), about 5e-8 here, so the outer numerator is 5e-28 while the inner central difference has a roundoff
floor of eps/h = 1e-40/1e-13 = 1e-27. The numerator sits below the noise: the entire position block of the
Jacobian is noise. That is why the failure gets worse as more atoms become interior, which is exactly the
direction of increasing A, and why ten atoms converged where eleven did not.
REPAIR. The derivative has a closed form. With P_x(y) = e^-x x^y / y!, d log P/dx = y/x - 1 and the identity
sum_y P (y/x - 1) = E[y]/x - 1 = 0 removes the second term, leaving
    D'(x) = sum_y P_x(y) (y/x - 1) [log P_x(y) - log Q(y)],  exact.
Implemented in `support_mp2.py` with a damped Newton step, and verified against a central difference at three
interior points to a relative agreement of 1e-25, 4e-25 and 2e-24. The A = 100 decision at K = 10, 11, 12 is
being re-run with it (`q32_A100_mp2.py`), with K = 10 as the control that must reproduce 8.4e-25.
PRE-REGISTERED READING, fixed before the run finishes: eleven converges and twelve does not (or twelve loses a
weight) means N*(100) = 11; both converge healthily with C(12) > C(11) means 12; both converge healthily without
a capacity gain means degenerate and the amplitude stays open; eleven failing again means the instrument is
still inadequate and A = 100 is reported as beyond reach.

## Amendment 14 (2026-09-05 01:10) - A = 100 SETTLED at eleven, and the certificate is now the sufficient condition
The repaired solver (analytic D') was run at K = 10, 11, 12 from the pre-registered reading in Amendment 13.
  K = 10: Newton residual 7.13e-29, converged, but D rises 2.589e-5 ABOVE C inside a gap. Ten atoms are not
          optimal, and this is the control that reproduces the old solver's converged point (8.4e-25 there).
  K = 11: Newton residual 6.13e-39. D equals C at all eleven atoms to 2.47e-16, and C - D >= 1.2496e-6 > 0 in
          every one of the ten gaps. Weights 0.033 to 0.163, spacings 2.44 to 25.33, all distinct.
  K = 12: Newton makes no progress (residual 7.80e-7) and D rises 5.06e-8 above C. No twelve-atom KKT point.
C(11) - C(10) = 6.189e-7 and C(12) - C(11) = -2.63e-10.
VERDICT: N*(100) = 11. This matches the very first answer of 2026-09-04, before five instruments in a row got
it wrong.
WHY THIS IS STRONGER THAN EVERY EARLIER ATTEMPT. The KKT condition for this channel is necessary AND sufficient:
an input is capacity-achieving exactly when D(x) = KL(P_x || Q) <= C on [0, A] with equality on the support. So
a single converged solution whose D never rises above C settles the count by itself. No comparison with
neighbouring K, no floor band, no two-sided heuristic. Everything before this was a comparison dressed as a test.
HOW THE CHECK IS DONE, since a grid cannot do it. D equals C at every atom and dips between them, so the whole
question is the sign of C - D inside each gap. With 1500 grid points and curvature about 5e-8 a peak can hide
between samples by roughly 3e-11, five orders above the solver's residual. Instead the critical point inside
each gap is located by bisecting the analytic D' to 1e-32 and C - D is evaluated there (`q32_certify.py`). The
reported "slack 5.63e-16" from the grid was therefore measuring D(0) - C at the first atom, not a maximum.
CONSEQUENCE. The four earlier amplitudes were certified by the floor-band heuristic and must be re-certified by
the sufficient condition, and the staircase can now be extended, which is exactly the condition Amendment 10 set
for going past A = 100.

## Amendment 15 (2026-09-05 01:40) - the certificate checker itself was wrong and issued a FALSE certificate
The re-certification sweep returned N*(20) = 3 and N*(30) = 5 against the established 5 and 6. That is not a
new staircase, it is a broken checker, and it was caught by the control rather than by inspection.
THE BUG. `q32_certify.certify` decided each gap from the sign of D' at the two ends. Opposite signs meant one
interior critical point, located by bisection. Equal signs were read as "D is monotone across this gap", and in
that branch it reported C minus the MINIMUM of D. Two things break that reading. First, D'(x) has a logarithmic
singularity as x approaches 0 (the y = 1 term carries log x), so the sample at the left end of the first gap is
large and negative and says nothing about the interior. Second, a gap may hold a maximum AND a minimum, which
gives equal end signs. Either way the gap goes down the monotone branch, where reporting the minimum hides the
maximum the test exists to find. At A = 20 the three-atom solution was certified although D rises 0.58 above C
at x = 1.35, which the direct scan shows plainly.
THE CORRECTION assumes nothing about the shape: sample D at 400 interior points of each gap, take the largest,
and if it falls on an interior sample bracket it with its neighbours and bisect D' to place the peak exactly.
STATUS OF AMENDMENT 14. Its conclusion N*(100) = 11 is now UNDER RE-TEST, and so is every gap number quoted in
it. What does NOT depend on the broken checker, and still stands: the Newton residuals (6.13e-39 at eleven atoms,
7.13e-29 at ten, no convergence at twelve), the capacities, C(11) - C(10) = 6.189e-7, and the diagnosis and
repair of the derivative in Amendment 13. What DOES depend on it is the claim that D never rises above C for the
eleven-atom solution, which is the whole certificate. The corrected checker is being run on all three, with the
falsely certified A = 20 solution as the control that must now fail by about 0.58.
The sweep results in `results_q32_sweep_mp2.json` are discarded.
LESSON, and it is the same one as yesterday in a new costume. A checker needs its own control. The sweep only
caught this because it was run on amplitudes whose answer was already known; had it been run first on A = 150,
where nothing is known, it would have produced a confident and wrong staircase.

## Amendment 19 (2026-09-05 03:25) - the sweep's weak link identified, and the instrument replaced by continuation

REPLACEMENT INSTRUMENT. Continuation in A, which never needs a fresh start. From a certified solution, a small
step in A lands inside the next basin; positions carry across by x -> x (A_new / A_old), exact in the
variance-stabilising coordinate t = sqrt(x); Newton polishes; and where the certificate fails a new atom is
inserted at the violation with a SMALL weight, which is the correct perturbation because at a transition
amplitude the new mass point appears with zero weight. The output is finer than isolated amplitudes: it is the
amplitude at which each new mass point appears.

THE FAILURE AT A = 120, and it is this project's recurring failure wearing new clothes. The inner loop inserted
an atom whenever the certificate failed, up to three times, WITHOUT first asking whether the solution it was
judging had converged. Newton returned a residual of 3.2e-4 there, so its D - C carried no information, and the
loop answered by adding atoms until K = 14. That is exactly the over-counting of 2026-09-04: a procedure that
adds elements in response to a signal that may be instrument failure. The K = 12, 13, 14 rows are discarded.
THE GUARD, now in `q32_continuation2.py`. An atom is inserted ONLY when the current solution has converged
(residual below 1e-25) and its D still rises above C. On a stall nothing is added; the amplitude step is halved
and the transition is approached more slowly, so the new mass point emerges carrying the small weight it
actually has near the transition. At most one atom per step, and the seed weight is tried from 1e-6 upward
rather than 1e-3 downward.

## Amendment 21 (2026-09-05 05:10) - N*(150) = 13, certified, and the insertion route has a structural limit
A = 150. The double-precision K-sweep gave K = 13 the smallest slack with healthy weights, which is NOT evidence
(the same sweep gives that pattern at K = 10 for A = 100, where the answer is 11). Decided instead by the
sufficient condition: K = 12 converges to 6.402e-35 and D rises 1.79e-4 above C at x = 39.106, so twelve is not
enough; inserting one atom at that violation with seed weight 1e-3 gives a thirteen-atom solution with Newton

THE STRUCTURAL LIMIT OF INSERTION, which is why the transition amplitudes can only be bracketed. Seeding the new
atom at 1e-5 and 1e-4 returned its weight EXACTLY at the seed (1.00e-05 and 1.00e-04) with residuals 9.8e-5 and
6.3e-4: Newton did not move it at all. The reason is structural. A near-zero weight contributes almost nothing
to the output law, so the Jacobian column for that weight is almost zero and the system is near-singular. Newton
therefore cannot resolve an atom at the moment of its birth, which is exactly the regime near a transition
amplitude. Seed 1e-3 worked at A = 150 because 150 sits well above the transition, where the new atom already
carries weight 0.057. Consequence, stated as a limit of the method rather than a fact about the channel:
transition amplitudes can be BRACKETED (eleven certified at A = 115, the best eleven-atom solution converged and
violating at A = 115.625, so the first transition lies in (115, 115.625]) but not located, and any K+1 solution
must be built at an amplitude comfortably above the transition.

## Amendment 26 (2026-09-05 09:10) - an independent check on N*(100), by descending instead of ascending
PRE-REGISTERED before the run. Going up, an atom is BORN with near-zero weight, its Jacobian column vanishes,
and Newton cannot resolve it (Amendment 21). Going down, an atom DIES: its weight shrinks toward zero and
removing a near-zero-weight atom is a small perturbation to the output law, which is exactly the change the
Jacobian handles well. So the direction that blocked the upward path should clear the downward one, and the
descent is a genuinely different route to the same answer rather than a repetition.
THE TEST. Start from the certified thirteen-atom solution at A = 150 and descend to A = 100, dropping an atom
whenever its weight falls below 1e-6 and re-converging. Since the KKT condition is necessary and sufficient and
the mutual information is concave in the input, a certified solution is the global optimum, so the descent MUST
arrive at A = 100 on the same eleven atoms certified there by the ascending route.

  path, and the certificate stands.
  Arrives at twelve healthy atoms with capacity above 1.759640325188972: the A = 100 certificate is WRONG and
  everything resting on it is withdrawn.
  Arrives at eleven atoms but with a different capacity: one of the two solutions is not the optimum and both
  need re-examining.
  Stalls before reaching 100: the check is inconclusive and says nothing either way.
SECOND CHECK FOR FREE. The ascent bracketed the eleven-to-twelve transition in (115.258, 115.31]. The descent
must lose its twelfth atom inside that same interval, from the other side. Agreement would be a strong internal
consistency check on the whole continuation machinery; disagreement would mean one of the two directions is
finding a non-optimal branch.

## Amendment 27 (2026-09-05 09:35) - the pre-registered expectation about the descent is PARTLY FALSIFIED
Amendment 26 predicted that the downward path would be well conditioned where the upward one is not, because an
atom dying is a small perturbation while an atom being born is invisible to the Jacobian. The first descent run
tested that and it is not right. Descending from the certified thirteen atoms at A = 150 the smallest weight
fell 5.35e-2, 4.63e-2, 3.91e-2, 3.10e-2 at A = 145, 140, 137.5, 135.875, all certified, and then Newton stalled
at A = 135 and again at 134.25, long before the weight came anywhere near the 1e-6 drop threshold. The KKT
system goes near-singular as an atom dies, not only as one is born.
WHAT THE ASYMMETRY ACTUALLY IS, corrected. The descent has no better conditioning than the ascent. What it has
is a cheap and TESTABLE move at the stall: drop the smallest atom and let the certificate judge the reduced
solution. Dropping is testable in a way that inserting is not, because the reduced system has one fewer unknown
and nothing new to place, whereas an insertion has to guess both a position and a weight in a regime where the
Jacobian carries no information about either. So the descent remains the better route, for a weaker and more
specific reason than the one written down before the run.

26 are UNCHANGED: arriving at A = 100 on eleven certified atoms with the same capacity confirms N*(100) = 11;
arriving on twelve healthy atoms with capacity above 1.759640325188972 refutes the certificate; and the descent
must lose its twelfth atom inside (115.258, 115.31] to agree with the ascent.

## Amendment 29 (2026-09-05 10:55) - the transition is an atom MERGE, which explains BOTH dead ends
Descending with twelve atoms from A = 132.68 to A = 116.28, the gap to the LEFT of the lightest atom shrinks
10.124, 9.828, 9.404, 8.757, 7.618, 6.486, 5.357, 4.248, 3.761, while its neighbouring gaps hold near 8.4 and
its weight falls only from 0.0634 to 0.0299. A weight of 0.03 does not reach zero within one unit of amplitude;
a separation of 3.76 shrinking by about one unit per unit of amplitude does. The twelve-to-eleven transition is
two atoms COALESCING, not one atom dying.
THIS EXPLAINS BOTH FAILURES AT ONCE, and corrects Amendment 21. Going up, an atom is not born out of nothing:
an existing atom SPLITS into two. So inserting a fresh low-weight atom at the violation was never the right
perturbation, and the seeds that came back untouched at 1e-5 and 1e-4 were not evidence of a singular Jacobian
so much as evidence that the move had the wrong shape. Going down, deleting one atom of a coalescing pair and
keeping the other is equally the wrong shape. The right moves are SPLIT and MERGE.
Amendment 21 said Newton cannot resolve an atom at its birth. The sharper and more useful statement is that the
perturbation must match the bifurcation: at a merge, replace the pair by one atom at their weight-weighted
centroid; at a split, replace one atom by a close pair. Whether a genuine birth-at-the-boundary also occurs at
other amplitudes is a separate question this run does not answer.

values from 14 to 58, so 15%. Extrapolated merge amplitudes from consecutive pairs give 114.85 and 115.01. The
ascending bracket from the other direction is (115.258, 115.310]. These are close but the extrapolation lands
slightly BELOW the bracket, and since the closest descent point is still a full unit from the transition and the
residuals carry visible curvature, the extrapolation is not accurate enough to call that a disagreement. It is
also not accurate enough to call it agreement. The decisive test is not the fit but whether the merge move
crosses the transition, which is running now (`q32_merge_test.py`).
NOTE ON THE OTHER TRANSITION. At the thirteen-to-twelve transition the drop move was accepted by the
certificate at A = 132.68, and there the lightest weight had fallen 5.35e-2, 4.63e-2, 3.91e-2, 3.10e-2, 2.48e-2,

recorded as unresolved rather than assumed either way.

THE FIX, and every term is in closed form. With g(x,y) = log P_x(y) - log Q(y),
    Dpp(x)      = sum_y P(x,y) [(y/x - 1)^2 - y/x^2] g(x,y) + 1/x

    dD(x)/dx_k  = -sum_y P(x,y) w_k P(x_k,y)(y/x_k - 1)/Q(y)
    dDp(x)/dw_k = -sum_y P(x,y)(y/x - 1) P(x_k,y)/Q(y)
    dDp(x)/dx_k = -sum_y P(x,y)(y/x - 1) w_k P(x_k,y)(y/x_k - 1)/Q(y)
with Dp and Dpp added on the diagonal where the evaluation point is the atom being varied. Weights are carried
unnormalised with sum w = 1 as its own residual row, so no normalisation term contaminates the entries.

## Amendment 48 (2026-09-05 17:00) - the certificate turned from an assertion into a computation, and a hole found
The fragility list put the certificate first: everything rests on sampling D at 400 points inside each gap, and
the claim that D is too smooth to hide a peak between samples was asserted, never measured. Two classical bounds
close that, using derivatives that are exact here.
  AWAY FROM ATOMS, the chord bound: if |D''| <= M2 on [s, s+h] then D(x) <= max(D(s), D(s+h)) + (M2/8) h^2 for
  all x in the interval. So if both sampled endpoints sit that far below C, no peak can hide, whatever its width.
  AT AN INTERIOR ATOM the chord bound is useless because D equals C there. Instead expand to third order, using
  D(a) = C and D'(a) = 0 from the KKT equations: D(a+d) <= C + (1/2)D''(a)d^2 + (M3/6)|d|^3, which stays at or
  below C for every |d| <= 3|D''(a)|/M3. That radius is computed, not assumed.
WHAT THE COMPUTATION FOUND, and the second item is a hole in our own argument.
  1. The SECOND-ORDER CONDITION had never been checked. The solver imposes D' = 0 at interior atoms, which a
     local MINIMUM satisfies just as well. All nine interior atoms at A = 100 have D'' < 0, from -0.0167 down to
     -8.30e-7, so they are genuine maxima. That check should have existed from the start.
  2. The chord bound FAILS on the first gap [0, 2.443]. There M2 = 13.567 against 1e-6 to 1e-2 in the interior
     gaps, so with 400 samples (M2/8)h^2 = 6.33e-5 swamps the observed margin of 3.13e-7. Near x = 0 the
     function is steep and sharply curved and a uniform grid is the wrong instrument. Every other gap passes,
     several by four orders.
  3. The two BOUNDARY atoms were mislabelled by the first version, which applied the interior test to them. At
     x = 0 and x = A the condition is one-sided, and D'' = 6.7e16 at x = 0 is just the 1/x term of D'' blowing
     up, which says nothing about optimality.
THE REPAIR uses the steepness instead of fighting it: if D' < 0 throughout an interval then D is decreasing and
cannot exceed its left endpoint, whatever happens between samples, and sampling D' with |D''| bounded makes that
rigorous, since the sign of D' cannot flip between samples while |D'| exceeds M2 h / 2. The same runs at x = A
with the sign reversed. `q32_certificate_bound2.py`.

## Amendment 49 (2026-09-05 17:40) - the certificate is now a COMPUTATION, and the first fragility is answered
At A = 100, eleven atoms, D <= C on the whole of [0, A] now follows from inequalities that cover every point of
the interval, with no appeal to the sampling being fine enough to catch a narrow peak.
  (i) MONOTONE RUNS inward from the boundary atoms, where the chord bound cannot work because D equals C there
      and the cubic radius is unavailable because D' is not zero. On a GEOMETRIC grid out from x = 0 the sign of
      D' is certified negative on (0, 0.2134] with worst margin |D'| / (M2 h / 2) = 1.935; on a uniform grid back
      from x = A it is certified positive on [93.4922, 100) with margin 2.176. Since D equals C at both boundary
      atoms, monotonicity puts D strictly below C throughout both runs. The remaining sliver (0, 1e-8] is covered
      by the expansion D(x) - C = x(log x + c) + O(x^2), which is negative there for any bounded c because
      log(1e-8) = -18.4.
  (ii) CUBIC SAFE RADIUS at each interior atom, from D''(a) < 0 and a bound on |D'''|: radii 0.616, 2.051, 3.055,
      2.989, 3.910, 3.520, 5.643, 7.057, 6.759. Two gaps are covered end to end by these alone.
  (iii) CHORD BOUND on every remaining subinterval, on a grid uniform in t = sqrt(x) with each subinterval
      judged by its own curvature. Worst slack over all of them 9.909e-6, and every one passes.
WHAT THE EXERCISE FOUND ALONG THE WAY, both of which are corrections to earlier work.
  The SECOND-ORDER CONDITION had never been checked in this project. The solver imposes D' = 0 at interior
  atoms, which a local MINIMUM satisfies equally well, so a solution could have passed every earlier test while
  sitting at a minimum. All nine interior atoms at A = 100 have D'' < 0, from -0.0167 to -8.30e-7, so they are
  genuine maxima; but the check should have existed from the first certificate and did not.
  The coordinate matters and we got it wrong twice. A uniform grid in x fails near zero because |D''| grows like
  1/x; a grid uniform in t = sqrt(x) also fails there, because its spacing goes like sqrt(x) and M2 h^2 stays
  constant; only a geometric grid, where the spacing goes like x, closes it. Version 4 then misread its own
  output, treating the sign change of D' at the interior dip as a failure when it is the expected end of the
  monotone region.
CONSEQUENCE. Item 1 of the fragility list in the audit package is answered at A = 100, and the same script runs
at A = 150. Everything that rests on the certificate rests on firmer ground than it did, and the fragility list
should be re-ordered accordingly.

## Amendment 60 (2026-09-05 22:50) - a VIOLATION LAW, and our side-observation was wrong in an instructive way

approaches its transition. A controlled sweep says otherwise. Holding the atom count at nine and raising the
amplitude above the known transition:

opposite of what the six heterogeneous points suggested. So the reading was wrong, and the reason matters: those
six came from different construction methods. The four sitting at x = 2.4 with violations of 5.8e-4 to 1.6e-3
were built by multi-start, and a slightly suboptimal solution violates first where the curvature is largest,
which is at the first interior atom. The two built by continuation violate in the middle of the support, where

METHODS. None of the bracket conclusions is affected, since a violation is a violation however the solution was
found.
WHAT THE CONTROLLED SWEEP GIVES INSTEAD is a clean power law, violation = c (A - Astar)^b with b measured at
1.46, near 3/2.

so the method needs points close to Astar. Those are the cheap ones: a K-atom solution just above its transition
comes from continuation, while the K+1 certificate that would otherwise be needed is exactly what the ceiling
forbids.
THE TEST THAT MATTERS is therefore at the ceiling, and it is running: locate the 13-to-14 transition from
thirteen-atom violations alone and see whether it lands in (152.000, 152.750]. If it does, transition-finding
stops being limited by the K = 13 ceiling.

count, which at K = 13 means the 13-to-14 transition at A* = 152.5003, confirmed inside the certified bracket.
It cannot go a step further, because that would need fourteen-atom violating solutions, which are the very
thing the ceiling withholds. So it is an extension by exactly one transition, not a way around the ceiling.
ADDENDUM TO AMENDMENT 65 (00:35). Levenberg-Marquardt finished: residual 3.776e-7 down to 7.518e-10 in 80 steps
and 937 seconds, then flat, the last six values being 7.34e-10, 7.49e-10, 7.49e-10, 7.51e-10, 7.50e-10,
7.50e-10. Three orders better than the SLSQP route and, for the first time on any fourteen-atom configuration,
at or below the basin threshold measured earlier (a start within about 1e-9 lets Newton converge, 1e-8 does
not). The script did not save the configuration, because it saved only on certification, so the chain is being
rerun with saving at every stage and plain Newton applied from the LM plateau. That is the decisive test: if
Newton's quadratic convergence takes over from 7.5e-10, the ceiling breaks; if Newton also stops at the plateau,
the plateau belongs to the system and not to the solver. The pre-registered reading is unchanged.

## Amendment 66 (2026-09-06 01:10) - the LM plateau belongs to the system, and the ceiling stands
From the informed split's best configuration at A = 152.60, Levenberg-Marquardt reached residual 7.528e-10 in
120 steps (1239 s) and flattened: 7.526e-10, 7.537e-10, 7.529e-10, 7.527e-10, 7.544e-10, 7.531e-10. Newton from
that point made NO progress at all: one step, residual unchanged at 7.528e-10. Every stage was saved this time
(`results_q32_lm_newton.json`).
So the plateau is not a property of LM's slow convergence, which was the earlier reading; it is a property of
the KKT system at this configuration. The pre-registered reading of Amendment 62 applies: no converged and
certified fourteen-atom solution, and THE K = 13 CEILING STANDS.
WHY THIS POINT, and it fits everything else. The independent audit rebuilt the 13-to-14 bracket to (152.50, 152.60],
so A = 152.60 sits at most 0.1 above the transition. At the transition the two daughter atoms of the split are
degenerate and the Jacobian is singular; 0.1 above it they are barely apart, the Jacobian is nearly singular,
and a residual floor of 7.5e-10 is what a near-singular system leaves. The audit saw the same thing from the
other side: its own ten-atom continuation stalled everywhere in (81.8, 82.0), just above the 9-to-10 transition,
so the stall is about PROXIMITY TO A TRANSITION as much as about K. The informed split's scan at A = 153.25,
further from the transition, reached only 3.4e-6, which says that going further out trades the singularity for
the basin problem.
WHAT THIS LEAVES. The best fourteen-atom residual on record is 7.528e-10, three to four orders better than any
route before the informed split, and it is not a certificate. The named remedy is unchanged.

## Amendment 69 (2026-09-06) - M2 and M3 turned from sampled maxima into proved bounds
Amendment 68 left one stated limit. The constants M2 = max|D''| and M3 = max|D'''| in the three pieces of the
certificate were sampled maxima. They are now interval enclosures (`support_iv.py`, `q32_certificate_v3.py`).
THE INSTRUMENT. mpmath's interval context evaluates every operation with directed rounding. An expression on
an interval X therefore encloses its value at every x in X. The closed forms D^(n) = sum_y P h_n g + c_n were
extended to order six by the recurrence h_{n+1} = h_n' + h_n(u - 1), c_{n+1} = E[h_n(U - 1)] + c_n', with the
expectation through Touchard moments; c_n = (-1)^n (n-2)!/x^(n-1). Two checks could have refuted the tables.
sympy regenerates them from the recurrence and they match at every order. Each closed form agrees with a
central difference of the previous order to 1e-21 at x = 0.7 and to 1e-29 or better at x >= 5. Everything
downstream of the decimal input is enclosed: P, Q, log Q, log y!, C = I(F), the point values, every
derivative. The y-sum truncation has a rigorous geometric tail bound (order 3 at x_lo = 1e-8: 5e-38).
WHAT THE FIRST PROVED VERSION TAUGHT. The naive interval sum over-estimates the range of D'' by 0.29 h on a
cell of width h at x = 20, where the true range is 6e-8 for h = 0.05. The y-terms cancel by four orders and the
enclosure adds their widths. The centered form f(X) in f(m) + f'(X)[-h/2, h/2] over-estimates at order h^2.
Each further level of recursion gains about five times, not an order of magnitude, because the naive
over-estimate itself grows about five times per derivative order. Depth 1 with 32 fixed pieces therefore
FAILED at A = 100. M3 at the flat atoms came out 20 to 500 times too large (atom 5, x = 27.09: 4.5e-4 against
1.08e-6 sampled). The cubic radii collapsed (0.0055 against 2.30). The chord cells next to those atoms lost by
1e-9 to 1e-8 on five gaps. That was an instrument failure and is recorded as one: the v2 values show the true
constants, and the fix is resolution, since the over-estimate at depth k scales as h^(k+1).
THE REPAIR. Depth 3, with closed forms to order six. The pieces over each radius interval are refined until
the enclosure is within 1.5x of the sampled maximum; the samples steer the cost and the enclosure carries the
proof. The radius is the largest certified member of a halving sequence, refined by three upward bisections.
The fixed-point iteration of v2 had oscillated between 0.0045 and 2.1 once M3 depended on the piece width.
A first candidate reaching the boundary atom at 0 wasted twelve minutes, so the sequence starts at gap/4.
A chord cell whose slack is negative is split to four levels before it is called a failure.
WHAT IS NOW PROVED, and what is not. For the decimal input F with K atoms: max_x D(x) <= I(F) + eta on all
of [0, A]. Here eta is the KKT residual of the decimal input, reported: 5.2e-16 at A = 100. It is set by the
17-digit float storage of the solution, not by the 1e-28 Newton residual it was computed to. By the standard
bound C(A) <= max_x D(x; F), F is within eta of capacity. The step from "an eta-optimal K-atom input" to "the
optimum has exactly K atoms" is the audit's caveat 1 and is still not made.

## Amendment 70 (2026-09-06) - the audit's caveat 1 closed. From the numerical KKT point to the exact one
Amendment 69 proved max_x D(x; F) <= I(F) + eta for the DECIMAL input F, with eta its KKT residual. The step
the audit named as caveat 1 remained: the exact optimum is not F, and nothing yet said it has K atoms. Two
computations close it (`q32_krawczyk.py`, `q32_certificate_v4.py`).
STEP ONE, EXISTENCE. The KKT equality system G(w, x) = 0 has 2K - 2 equations in 2K - 2 unknowns:
D(x_i) = D(x_0) for i = 1..K-1, sum w = 1, and D'(x_i) = 0 at the K - 2 interior atoms, with x_0 = 0 and
x_{K-1} = A fixed. Its analytic Jacobian (support_mp3) is evaluated in interval arithmetic over the box
B = {|w_k - w~_k| <= rho, |x_i - x~_i| <= rho} around the 40-digit numerical point x~. The Krawczyk operator
K(B) = x~ - Y G(x~) + (I - Y J(B))(B - x~), with Y the floating inverse of J(x~), lies strictly inside B
whenever max_i (|Y G(x~)|_i + rho sum_j |I - Y J(B)|_ij) < rho. Then G has exactly one zero F* in B
(Krawczyk 1969; Moore 1977; Neumaier 1990, Thm 5.1.7). The ladder at A = 100: rho = 1e-36 FAILS (the shift
|Y G| = 2.7e-34 does not fit), rho = 1e-30, 1e-20, 1e-10 pass (ratios 2.7e-4, 2.2e-12, 0.021), rho = 1e-3
fails (contraction 2e5). So F* exists, is unique in the box of radius 1e-10, and lies within 1e-30 of x~.
Two things had to be fixed first, and are recorded. The stored solutions carried x_0 = 1.5e-17 instead of 0
(an artefact of the first solver, never moved by Newton), which made D'(x_0) = log(1e-17) = -36.7 a row of
the system; the boundary atoms are now snapped to exactly 0 and A before re-convergence (residual 7e-39 in
two Newton steps). And a float amplitude such as 39.612 is not the decimal 39.612 stored as the last atom; the
amplitude is read as that decimal, and the set of free atoms is fixed once with a tolerance, so the point
system and the box system have the same unknowns (an IndexError caught the mismatch).
STEP TWO, THE CERTIFICATE FOR F*. The three-piece argument is run with the PARAMETERS AS THE BOX, so every
enclosure covers F*. For F* the KKT rows are exact: D(x_k; F*) = C(F*) at every atom and D'(a*; F*) = 0 at
every interior atom. Piece (i) gives D(x; F*) <= D(0; F*) = C(F*) near 0 and D(x; F*) <= D(A; F*) = C(F*)
near A. Piece (ii) at an interior atom a* in [a~ - rho, a~ + rho]: sup_B D''(a) < 0 and |D'''| <= M3 on
[a~ - rho - r, a~ + rho + r] for every F in B, so D(x; F*) <= C(F*) for |x - a*| <= r, which covers
[a~ - (r - rho), a~ + (r - rho)] whatever a* is. Piece (iii) on every remaining cell: D(x; F*) <=
sup_B[max(D(s0), D(s1)) + M2 h^2/8] <= inf_B C(F) <= C(F*). No eta appears anywhere. A precision-order bug
was caught by the consistency numbers printed for exactly this purpose: the 40-digit strings were parsed
before the precision was raised, the box was centred on a 15-digit point, and D(0) - C over the box came out
3.8e-17 instead of the 1e-29 a 1e-30 box on twenty parameters allows; fixed, the numbers read 8e-29.
WHAT FOLLOWS. D(x; F*) <= C(F*) on all of [0, A] is the KKT sufficient condition, so F* is capacity-achieving
(Smith 1971; Shamai 1990 for the Poisson channel). The capacity-achieving input is unique: Shamai 1990 (IEE Proc. I
137(6):424-430), cited for exactly this by Barletta, Dytso and Shamai 2024 (arXiv 2401.05045, p. 1: "the
optimizing input distribution is unique and discrete with finitely many mass points", also with dark current);
the mechanism is strict concavity of I in the output law plus identifiability of finite Poisson mixtures.
Hence F* is THE optimum, it has K atoms, and N*(A) = K exactly. What stays outside the
computation: those two theorems, the Krawczyk theorem, and the correctness of mpmath's directed rounding.
THE CONTROL, A = 100, K = 11, rho = 1e-30: PROVED, 2076 s.
    Krawczyk: n = 20 unknowns, |G(x~)| = 7.7e-39, |Y| = 1.75e6, shift 2.7e-34, contraction 2.1e-22, ratio 2.7e-4.

## Amendment 71a (2026-09-06) - two coverage gaps in piece (i), found by review after the pass, closed
Amendments 69 and 70 passed. A review of what each piece of the argument actually covers, done after the
pass and not before, found two places where piece (i) did not check what it claimed.
GAP ONE. The left run started at x = 1e-8 and the decade sweep of Amendment 69 stopped at 1e-300. Nothing
checked (0, 1e-300). The sweep was also the wrong tool. It relied on interval evaluation near 0, where the closed forms
carry 1/x^j and cannot stay tight. It is replaced by a LEMMA with computed constants. The lemma holds on all
of (0, x1] for x1 = 1e-8. Write D'(x) = sum_y P(x,y)(y/x - 1) g(x,y). The y = 0 term is
e^{-x}(x + log Q(0)), negative because Q(0) < 1 and x < -log Q(0). The y = 1 term is
(1 - x)e^{-x}(log x - x - log Q(1)). Its second factor is negative and at most log x1 - log Q(1)_lo. Its first
factor lies in [(1 - x1)e^{-x1}, 1]. So the term is at most (1 - x1)e^{-x1}(log x1 - log Q(1)_lo). Every term
with y >= 2 is at most (x^{y-1}/(y-1)!)(y|log x| + x + log y! + |log Q(y)|). On (0, x1] with x1 < 1/e the
factor x^{y-1}|log x| is increasing, so each term is bounded by its value at x1. Beyond ny the enclosed Q(y)
is replaced by log(1/w_A) + A + log y!. The terms then fall by a factor at most 2 x1/y each, a geometric tail.
The bound is evaluated in interval arithmetic (`q32_piece_i.py`, left_sliver).
GAP TWO. The right grid started at A - h. The cell (A - h, A] was exempt from the chord bound because it
lies above right_reach. Nobody checked it. The grid now starts at A itself, so the first cell is
[A - h, A] and D'(A) > 0 is tested at the boundary atom.
Neither gap changed a verdict: D' is about -15 on the left sliver and the right margin is about 2. But the
certificate must check them, and now does. v3 and v4 use the corrected piece from now on. Piece (i) alone
was re-run at every certified endpoint, for the float input (Amendment 69 status) and for the Krawczyk box
(Amendment 70 status), with identical numbers (`q32_piece_i_fix.py`, about 40 s each):

Amendment 70 listed the correctness of mpmath's directed rounding among the things outside the computation.
That item is now reduced. python-flint's arb is Johansson's ball arithmetic, an implementation independent of mpmath.iv
with its own rounding and error propagation. It was installed, and the entire exact-point chain was
re-implemented on it (`q32_certificate_arb.py`). That chain is the Krawczyk inclusion, piece (i) with the
sliver lemma and the right grid from A, piece (ii) with depth-3 enclosures and adaptive pieces, and piece
(iii) on every non-exempt cell, all with the parameters as the box of radius 1e-30. The closed forms and coefficient tables
are shared with support_iv.py; every comparison is an arb comparison, true only when the balls prove it.
A first cross-check (`q32_arb_crosscheck.py`) put the two libraries side by side on the control cells.
Enclosure widths differ by 0.1 to 0.4 percent; both contain all samples; both overlap. On the binding gap
of A = 100 the arb worst slack is 1.036413e-6 against mpmath's 1.036413e-6, ratio 1.000000.

minutes). What remains outside the computation is now short. The KKT sufficiency theorem. The uniqueness theorem
(Shamai 1990). The Krawczyk theorem. And the proposition that two independent rigorous-arithmetic libraries
are wrong in the same way at the same digits.

input interval [lambda, A + lambda]. So the exact-point certificate applies with the left boundary atom at
lambda. The left end becomes a regular point, with no sliver lemma and a linear left grid from lambda. The
40-digit Newton pins both end atoms. Nothing else changes (`q35_dark_certify.py`, `results_q35_dark_certify.json`).

## Amendment 78 (2026-09-06) - N*(218.5) = 17 certified; the half-line function E(g)
The 17-atom branch walked from the birth point to A = 218.5 with the pure-Newton walker (steps 0.5 to
0.75; `q66_walk_pure.py`), re-solved at 50 digits and certified on arb at rho = 1e-30: Krawczyk ratio
1.3e-10, worst chord slack 3.4e-8, N*(218.5) = 17 PROVED (`results_q53b_certify17_A218.500.json`).
Eighteen amplitudes are certified. Struck: the A_18 bisection from this point (221.71), because the float64
re-solve still fails at a newborn weight of 0.029; the two valid bisections of the record used inputs with
smallest weight 0.043 and 0.052, so the rule is a smallest weight of 0.04 or more. A_18 is being measured
from the walked point at A = 236 (smallest weight 0.044).
Theory: the half-line problem (wall, thirty free atoms, frozen periodic tail of gap g) is solved cleanly
for both kernels at g = 1.43 to 1.75 (Statements 8 and 9 in CONJECTURE_LANE3). The displacement is
c = E(g)/2 with E the total excess length of the Poisson chain over the Gaussian one; E/2 is linear in g
(0.287 at 1.75 to 0.322 at 1.43, slope -0.109) and reproduces c(15) = 0.312 at g = 1.55. Since the
chain cannot hold a uniform bulk below g of about 1.43, c_infinity is 0.32 to 0.33 by this route, and
c(K) converges; the 1/K fit of Amendment 75 (asymptote 0.346) over-extrapolates by about 0.02.

Addendum to Amendment 78 (same morning): the sentence "c_infinity is 0.32 to 0.33 by this route ... the
1/K fit over-extrapolates by about 0.02" is withdrawn. It assumed the bulk gap tends to 1.41, twice the
current Gaussian transition spacing; the spacing itself is still falling (0.7646 to 0.7060 over K = 15 to
20, fitted by 0.534 + 3.58/K), so the limiting bulk gap, and with it c_infinity, depends on the growth law
of the number of atoms with A, which is not settled by the data. What the half-line problem does establish
is c(K) = E(g_eff(K))/2 with E linear in g on the measured range and the slope of c(K) in K reproduced
quantitatively (Statement 9 correction in CONJECTURE_LANE3).

The 17-atom branch walked to A = 236 (smallest weight 0.0445) is certified on arb at rho = 1e-30: Krawczyk

K = 18 was born from that branch by the feasibility-scaled unfolding (`q68_birth_feasible.py`, from the

rho = 1e-28: Krawczyk ratio 1.5e-9, worst chord slack 7.5e-12, N*(236.92) = 18 PROVED
(`results_q53b_certify18_A236.920.json`). Twenty amplitudes are certified, K = 5 to 18 without a gap.
The transition amplitude needs a better definition. The float64 bisection from the 236 point returned
A_18 = 236.9458, ABOVE the certified 18-atom point at 236.9199, which is impossible if A_18 is where the
17-atom optimum stops being optimal. `q79_verify_A18.py` settles it with 40-digit 17-atom KKT points: the
violation max(D - C) is 1.3e-13 at A = 236.85, 1.7e-13 at 236.90, 4.5e-10 at 236.93 and 1.6e-9 at 236.96,
in agreement with the float routine to 1e-13. So the float bisection is numerically right but its
threshold of 1e-9 on the violation sits about 0.03 above the true transition, because the violation grows
slowly (roughly quadratically) from zero. Every A_K of the record carries that bias, about +0.03 to +0.04
in A and +0.001 in c(K), and the births "0.043 above A_K" of Amendments 74 and 77 were largely the bias.
New definition, used from here on: A_{K+1} is the amplitude at which the newborn weight of the (K+1)-atom
KKT branch vanishes, obtained from the 40-digit unfolding at eps = 1e-3, 5e-4, 2.5e-4 by linear
extrapolation (`q80_AK_by_unfolding.py`). The old values are kept, labelled by their threshold, until the
new ones are computed for K = 15 to 18.

(tail weights 0.38, bulk gaps 0.98 to 1.71) and the compression limit near g = 1.43 is neither confirmed
nor refuted.

## Amendment 86 (2026-09-06) - refocus on the principle; the third channel and the mechanism
On review the main line moved from the count formula to the principle behind the
Poisson-Gaussian correspondence. Two results in one hour. (1) Third channel: the binomial B(n, p) on
[0, 1] (two Poisson-type degenerate endpoints, Fisher length pi sqrt(n)) has N_B(n) = N_G(pi sqrt(n)/2 -
0.60) at thirteen of sixteen resolved n in 30..100, the three departures being one count below the
prediction within 0.04 of a Gaussian transition (wall constant 0.31 to 0.32 per wall against 0.30 for
Poisson); the wall excess over the Gaussian input at n = 50 is 0.412, 0.107, 0.057, 0.024 against the
Poisson 0.407, 0.091, 0.047, 0.031 (`q94_binomial_universality.py`, `results_q94_binomial.json`;
Statement 12). (2) Mechanism: in the Fisher coordinate of a one-parameter exponential family,
KL(theta || theta + d) = d^2/2 - kappa_3 d^3/12 + O(d^4) with kappa_3 the skewness (Amari-Chentsov
tensor), verified exactly for Poisson and numerically for the binomial (Statement 13). The bulk of every
such channel is Gaussian to O(kappa_3) = O(1/scale); the wall is where kappa_3 = O(1); the binomial wall
near p = 0 has the Poisson profile kappa_3 = 2/tau, which is why the same wall constant appears. A negative
control is being run on the gamma (scale) family, whose skewness is constant along the interval.
The Poisson count chain continues in the background (K = 20 being born from the certified 19-atom branch).

Addendum to Amendment 86 (same afternoon): the binomial wall constant. With the refined Gaussian
transitions for K <= 14 the binomial counts bracket the total wall constant at c_tot = 0.717 +- 0.003 over
K = 9..12 (n = 30..58) and (0.64, 0.79] over K = 13..17: the law N_B(n) = N_G(pi sqrt(n)/2 - c_tot) holds
with one constant, but the constant is 0.36 per wall, not the Poisson 0.30; the sentence "with the Poisson
wall constant to 0.02 per wall" is withdrawn. The negative control (gamma family, constant skewness, no
degenerate endpoint) behaves as Statement 13 predicts: Gaussian walls and a second-order bulk shift
(Statement 14).

Measured from every stored near-birth state (newborn weight 1e-3 or less), offset of the newborn from its nearest
neighbour in the Fisher coordinate t = 2 sqrt(x), bulk spacing about 1.7:
| K | type | A | w_newborn | offset (Fisher) | file |
| 17 | insertion | 214.685 | 1e-3 | 0.609 | results_q68_K17_A214.685_exact40 |
| 19 | insertion | 259.982 | 1e-3 | 0.590 | results_q68_K19_A259.982_exact40 |

| 18 | split | 236.920 | 1e-3 | 0.202 | results_q68_K18_A236.920_exact40 |
| 20 | split | 283.668 | 1e-3 | 0.196 | results_q68_K20_A283.668_exact40 |
| 22 | split | 333.199 | 2.5e-4 | 0.184 | results_q80_state_K22_eps2.5e-4 |
The "split" birth of the Poisson channel is not a pitchfork: the new atom appears 0.18-0.20 Fisher units from an
existing atom, which stays (its weight is handed over; K dw/dA = 1.9 at birth, saturating at the pair mean). The
Gaussian even-K birth replaces the centre atom by a symmetric pair (a pitchfork forced by the reflection
symmetry); the Poisson channel has no such symmetry, so both birth types are ordinary tangencies of the KKT
function, at 0.19 (even K) or 0.58 (odd K) from the nearest atom. Both offsets fall slowly with K (0.61 -> 0.56,
0.20 -> 0.18 over K = 17..22). Consequence for the walker: after a split birth the newborn moves about 4 x-units
per unit A (sqrt onset fitted through the two rungs: x = 87.953 + 0.531 sqrt(A - 333.196)) while its weight
grows 0.088 per unit A, so a scaled guess fails (q122 is the structurally informed guess).

q134 (symmetry imposed; pair tracked on its sqrt law after the pitchfork): 17 -> 18 split at n*(18) = 101.75

c = E/2 = 0.30 per wall (the two-wall law assumed each wall costs E in total length, 2c = E in half-length).
The count deficit is therefore not visible gap by gap; it is the sum: two Poisson walls in one system cost
about 1.4 E each in total length, one Poisson wall (with a regular far end) costs E. Two readings, both

Gaussian reference profile itself depends on the half-length, so the excess sum depends on which Gaussian

reaches 7 gaps; at K = 18 the two tails overlap over the whole interior). Test to separate (a) from (b): a
one-wall Poisson channel with a deterministic far end far away (large K, e.g. K = 40, where the tails do not
overlap) against the two-wall law: if the lateness persists at large K, it is (a); if it vanishes, it is (b).

## Amendment 174 (2026-09-10 12:20) - pre-registration, the double-Poisson channel as the third two-wall case
Fact on the table (Amendment 173): with one transition rule the symmetric binomial channel's per-wall cost exceeds the
Poisson wall constant by 0.065-0.069 in half-length for K = 18-23 (n = 102-153), flat (a 1/n law would fall by a third
over this range). Two readings: (i) a two-wall property (the second wall costs more than the first, or the two wall
profiles interact through the interior); (ii) a property of the binomial kernel (the conditioning of two Poisson
counts on their sum, which removes the sum's information and changes the interior kernel while keeping the Fisher
geometry). Third case that separates them: the DOUBLE-POISSON channel Y = (Y1, Y2), Y1 ~ Poisson(x), Y2 ~ Poisson(A - x),
0 <= x <= A. It has Poisson walls at both ends (Y1 = 0 at x = 0; Y2 = 0 at x = A), Fisher information 1/x + 1/(A - x),
Fisher coordinate t = 2 sqrt(A) asin sqrt(x/A) and total length pi sqrt(A): exactly the binomial geometry with n = A,
but the unconditioned kernel. Predictions before the computation (q136, float mirror-reduced KKT with held-coordinate
births, A continuous so the transitions are bisected):
  (i) two-wall property: A*(22) = 141.99 and A*(23) = 152.67 (the binomial values; tolerance 0.3, one third of the
      H0-H1 gap);
  (ii) binomial-kernel property: A*(22) = 140.0 and A*(23) = 150.6 (H0 of Amendment 171: no excess);
  anything else (e.g. an excess of a different size) is recorded as such and neither reading is claimed.
The start state is the binomial K = 21 configuration at n = 141 mapped by the common Fisher coordinate.

## Amendment 175 (2026-09-10 12:50) - the double-Poisson channel is not a two-wall test; result recorded and the case dropped
q136 (float mirror-reduced KKT, A continuous, births by held-coordinate brackets, transitions bisected): starting from the
binomial K = 21 configuration at n = 141, the double-Poisson K = 21 point solves (residual 1e-13) but already has a
positive centre curvature at A = 141; stepping down, the K = 21 -> 22 split is at A* = 135.630 (bracket 135.6299 ..
135.6309), against the pre-registered (i) 141.99 and (ii) 140.0: neither; 4.4 below H0. Its wall gaps at A = 141 are
3.1156, 2.2403, 1.9594, 1.7987, 1.6932, all below the Poisson wall's 3.1278, 2.2688, 1.9954, 1.8423, 1.7457.
Reason, seen after the fact: with S = Y1 + Y2 ~ Poisson(A) independent of x, and Y1 | S ~ Bin(S, x/A), the
double-Poisson channel is the binomial channel with a random, receiver-known n ~ Poisson(A) (spread +-12 at A = 141),
one input distribution serving all n. It is not "two Poisson walls with the binomial geometry"; its transitions are
those of the n-mixture and its walls are the mixture's. The test of Amendment 174 is therefore void for the two-wall
question; the number stands as a fact about the mixture channel (a binomial channel with Poisson-distributed n has
MORE levels than the fixed-n binomial at the mean: 22 levels from A = 135.6 against n = 142.0) and the case is dropped.
Next third case (Amendment 176): the one-wall binomial channel on [0, rho n] at fixed K = 18 for rho = 0.3 .. 0.95,
which separates "the excess needs the second wall" from "the excess comes from the interior (the skew reversal at
p = 1/2 entering the range)".

## Amendment 183 (2026-09-10 17:15) - literature status of the binomial count, a published conjecture Theta(n^(3/4)), and the pre-registered count at n = 350 and 1000
Ground truth read today (rule 14): (i) Zieder, Favano, Barletta, Dytso, ISIT 2024 (arXiv:2401.12818): the symmetric binomial
channel's capacity-achieving input is unique; support size between order sqrt(n) and n/2; (ii) Baniasadi, Barletta, Dytso,
"An improved lower bound on support size of capacity-achieving inputs for the binomial channel: extended version",
arXiv:2605.12472 (12 May 2026): lower bound of order sqrt(n log log n), C(n) = (1/2) log(n pi / 2e) + o(1), the Beta(1/2,1/2)
reference input; (iii) Favano, Baniasadi, Zieder, Barletta, Dytso, arXiv:2607.02683 (v2, 3 Aug 2026), text extracted from the
PDF (papers_favano2026_2607.02683.txt): numerical CAIDs for n in {4, 10, 20, 30, ..., 350} by the dual method of Komninakis-
Vandenberghe-Wesel plus the DAB refinement (tolerance 1e-6), support cardinality shown in their Fig. 5 (no table in the
text); and the sentence "In [37], using numerical evidence, the authors conjectured that the real scaling of the number
of points is |supp(P_X*)| = Theta(n^(3/4))", [37] = Mattingly, Transtrum, Abbott, Machta, PNAS 2018 (our reference [19]).
No count law, no Fisher-length statement and no finite-K term appear in any of the three.
Our law says the count is the Gaussian count at h_eff = pi sqrt(n)/2 (1 + 0.42 (1 - 2/pi)/K) - 2 c(K), and the Gaussian
count grows as h times a slowly growing factor (Wang 2025: faster than h; Wang-Barletta-Dytso 2025: at least h sqrt(log h)).
Normalized at our K = 26 point (n = 186.386), the competing scalings give at n = 350: n^(3/4): 41.7; sqrt(n): 35.6;
sqrt(n) sqrt(log): 37.7; and at n = 1000: 91.7 / 60.2 / 69.2. PRE-REGISTERED: the KKT count
of the symmetric channel (q135 float-only continuation from n = 190, K = 26; results_q135_sym_bin_float_to1000.log) at
n = 350 is 36 to 38 under the Fisher picture and 41 to 42 under Theta(n^(3/4)); at n = 1000 it is 60 to 64 against 91 to 92.
A count at n = 350 of 40 or more, or at n = 1000 of 75 or more, would put the paper's picture in doubt. Favano et al.'s
Fig. 5 value at n = 350 (numerical, tolerance 1e-6) is read from the rendered page and recorded next to ours.

## Amendment 198 (2026-09-11 01:50) - the derivation program (pre-registered steps, each with a numerical test on data in hand)
Goal: turn c(K) = E(g_eff)/2 and E(g) = 0.984 - 0.2347 g from measured laws into consequences of the KKT equations.
Steps, in order, each closed by a test before the next:
T1. Information density in the Fisher coordinate. For the Poisson kernel write D(t) (t = 2 sqrt x) and expand around
    the Gaussian kernel of unit variance in t: D_P(t) = D_G(t) + (2/t) D_1(t) + (4/t^2) D_2(t) + ..., the coefficients
    from the cumulants of the Poisson law in the t variable (skewness 2/t: the Amari-Chentsov cubic term; kurtosis
    4/t^2 ... ). TEST: evaluate D_P and D_G on the SAME atom set (the certified 24-point at A = 385.63) and check that
    D_P - D_G scales as 2/t times a smooth function across the interior (t = 8 .. 39); report the residual after the
    first-order term.
T2. Linear response of the Gaussian lattice. Linearize the Gaussian chain's KKT equations (equal D, D' = 0) around
    the uniform lattice of spacing g: the Jacobian in (positions, weights) has decaying modes exp(-k/ell(g)) away
    from a perturbation. TEST: ell(g) from the Jacobian's eigen-structure against the measured decay of the Poisson
    excess per gap (Fig. 1b: geometric, ratio 0.48 .. 0.76 per ten gaps over g = 1.47 .. 1.99).
T3. Wall as source x response. Write the excess E(g) = sum_k delta_k(g) with delta_k = (source at the wall) x (lattice
    response). TEST: does a g-INDEPENDENT source (the first two Poisson gaps 3.126, 2.260, which barely move with g)
    combined with the g-dependent response ell(g) reproduce the slope dE/dg = -0.2347 with no fitted quantity? If yes,
    the linear law is derived to first order; if the slope comes out wrong, the source's own g-dependence is the next
    term.
T4. The count law. With E(g) in hand, N_P(A) = N_G(sqrt A - E(g_eff)/2) follows if the birth criterion (a violation at
    the centre of the largest gap) is the same function of the local gap in both channels; TEST: the birth gap at the
    Poisson births (Table II) against the Gaussian birth gap at A_g(K) (q143 data K <= 32): equal to 1e-3?
T5. The finite-K term (7): derive the kappa V/K correction from the dispersion-ratio gradient acting on the interior
    equations (T1 with r(x) varying); TEST: predict kappa's value; measured 0.42.
Each step's numbers go into a DERIVATION_LOG.md with the code that produced them (q150 onward).

## Amendment 211 (2026-09-11) - q154 is void; T5e must be built on q118, not on a fresh residual
q154 (T5e v2) reproduced the wall exactly (gap excess 0.4068, 0.0908, 0.0471, 0.0315 against the T4c reference
0.4068, 0.0908, 0.0470, 0.0310) but its chain excess did not saturate: the bulk gaps carried about 0.03 each,
giving E(1.4462) = 1.3547 where the m = 30 law predicts 0.6439. The trusted tool q118, run at g = 1.47, returns
E = 0.6376, the published value, with residuals 8e-14 (Poisson) and 1e-15 (Gaussian), and a cumulative excess
that plateaus: 0.5971, 0.6330, 0.6421, 0.6414, 0.6402 at k = 5, 8, 12, 16, 20. So the physics is unchanged and
q154's own Gaussian/Poisson solves are wrong by about 0.03 per bulk gap.
Cause, identified: q118 sizes the Gaussian quadrature grid from the actual chain (umax = u_init[-1] + g n_t + 8,
shift = umax/2), while q154 sized it from a formula in g. A mis-centred grid biases the Gaussian chain's bulk
spacing, and the bias shows up as a non-saturating excess. Two further q154 defects were found on the way: the
residual gate was tighter than each kernel's quadrature floor (the Gaussian bottoms out near 1e-8), and a
rewrite dropped the WALL_G/WALL_P constants.
DECISION: q154 is void as an instrument. T5e is rebuilt by adding the binomial kernel to q118's own residual
and grid construction, so that the binomial chain is solved by the machinery that reproduces the published
E(g) to 1e-14. Pre-registration of the measurement itself is unchanged from Amendment 209.

## Amendment 215 (2026-09-11) - is the 1/n term wall-local? The chain-length test, pre-registered

Fisher units long while the whole channel at n = 152 is pi sqrt(152) = 38.7, so the chain does not fit inside
the channel it is meant to model.

## Amendment 218 (2026-09-11) - a headline claim WITHDRAWN: we misread zeta = 3/4 as a count exponent
Reader 3 of the second IEEE draft reading reported that Section IV-D refutes a conjecture nobody made. Verified
at the source, arXiv:1710.09351 (Abbott and Machta, J. Stat. Phys. 176, 2019):
  equation (2):  rho_0 = K/L ~ L^(-1+1/zeta) = L^(1/3),  zeta = 3/4, so K ~ L^(1/zeta) = L^(4/3);
  equation (22): for a Fisher length growing as sqrt(m),  K ~ m^(1/(2 zeta)) = m^(2/3);
  figure 1:      the lines drawn are I = zeta log K for zeta = 1 and zeta = 3/4.
So 3/4 is the exponent in I = zeta log K, and the predicted count exponent in n is 2/3. Our draft carried
"Mattingly et al. conjectured Theta(n^(3/4))" and reported our measured 0.57 as a refutation of it. That claim
is WITHDRAWN. Against the correct asymptotic 2/3 our measurement is below, not contradictory in kind: doubling
n from 350 to 700 multiplies the count by 1.49 where 2/3 gives 1.59, and at n = 700 the Fisher length is 83
while the law is stated for L -> infinity, so a finite-size explanation is open. The paper now says exactly
that.
SECOND correction from the same source. Abbott and Machta write, comparing the binomial's Gaussian and Poisson
limits, that "the agreement of these very different models suggests that the zeta = 3/4 power is in some sense
universal, for nonsingular one-dimensional models", and they publish the wall weight ratios 0.63, 0.54, 0.49
as well as the positions we already cite. So the universality of the GROWTH is theirs, and our sentence "what
had not been stated is whether the two channels share their count law" was too strong. The novelty is now
stated as what it actually is: the correspondence level by level, the half-length at which it holds, and the
offset between the two counts.
This is the most consequential finding of the draft-reading programme so far, and it came from a referee that saw
only the manuscript.

## Amendment 221 (2026-09-11) - 220(b) resolved: not the tail, not the fit; a constant 0.003 in E remains
Tail length 10 to 80 at m = 30, g = 1.47: E(1.47) = 0.63764 in every case, shift below 1e-05, so the

## Amendment 222 (2026-09-11) - 221 resolved: the offset is the chain's resolution floor, not a new effect
Pre-registered branches were "below 0.0005 means the weight normalisation" and "above 0.002 means it is not".
Neither fired as stated, because the informative measurement turned out to be the sensitivity rather than the
substitution: dE/d(tail weight ratio) = -12.0 at ratio 1, measured by continuation (residuals 8e-14 and 2e-13;
larger steps left the basin and are not reported). The 0.0031 offset in E is what a tail-weight gradient of
0.026 percent per atom produces, and the full problem's bulk weights do carry a gradient where the chain
imposes none. So the offset is the resolution floor of the chain model, and the closure's rms of 0.0017 in c
sits at that floor rather than above it. No further derivation of the offset is warranted; what would be
warranted is a chain whose far boundary carries the real weight gradient, which is a different model.
