## Amendment 226 (2026-09-11) - the exponential law is WITHDRAWN as a derivation target
T5j: pinning the chain's frozen tail at absolute positions leaves the solution unchanged (residual 8e-14 both
ways) but changes the bump's total from +14.178 to +0.041, a factor of 350, while the first four gaps move by
0.7 percent. The total is therefore a gauge quantity, how far the free block slides against a tail that
follows it, and the law T(g) = T0 exp(-3.9 g) recorded in T5h and Amendment 217 describes the convention and
not the channel. It is withdrawn as a target. The same applies to the growth of a(m) with chain length in T5f.
What survives is the first four gaps, robust to 0.7 percent across conventions and reproduced by the pinned
linear response to between 0.1 and 3.8 percent. That is the object the derivation should close, and it is
finite and well conditioned. Beyond gap six the response is nonlinear in both conventions.

## Amendment 227 (2026-09-11) - round three, reader 5: the coordinate itself is published prior art
VERIFIED AT SOURCE and this is the important one. Anscombe, Biometrika 35 (1948) 246-254, gives the
variance-stabilising transforms of the Poisson, binomial AND negative-binomial laws, which are exactly the
three Fisher coordinates this paper uses. Tsiatmas, Willems and Baggen, ISIT 2013, "Square root approximation
to the Poisson channel", build an additive constant-variance Gaussian channel from the Poisson one by that
transform and prove the rates converge at large peak or average power. So neither the square-root coordinate
nor the Poisson-to-Gaussian correspondence is new, and the paper had not cited either. Both are now cited and
the Introduction states plainly that what those results give is an asymptotic equivalence, while what is
measured here is the finite-amplitude statement: the counts agree level by level once the half-length is
shortened by an explicit constant. This is the third time a draft reading has narrowed the novelty claim, after
Abbott and Machta's exponent (Amendment 218) and their weight ratios.
ALSO FIXED, all verified against our own tables: the Appendix row still wrote the finite-K term with a plus
after Amendment 219 corrected the equation, and now carries the minus; Section IV-J quoted -0.0016 in c, which
is the value under the REFITTED infinite-chain law, while the law the paper prints gives -0.0019 in c and
-0.0038 in E, and both are now stated with the law each belongs to; Section V's "two to three times the

## Amendment 229 (2026-09-11) - the g_eff choice: measured, argued, and disclosed
Both round-three referees called the definition of g_eff outcome-determining. Measured against the twenty
wall constants of Table II, closing with E(g) = 0.9840 - 0.2347 g:

| estimator of the local Gaussian spacing | closure rms | mean residual |
|---|---|---|
| symmetric difference A_g(K+1) - A_g(K-1), used here | 0.00172 | -0.00010 |
| one-sided difference 2[A_g(K+1) - A_g(K)] | 0.00452 | -0.00286 |
| mean level spacing 2 A_g(K)/(K-1) | 0.03123 | +0.02728 |

The argument, which the paper now carries: E(g) was fitted on chains of bulk spacing g, so the quantity to
feed it is the LOCAL length added per level at the birth. The global mean fails by a factor of eighteen
because the Gaussian atoms are not uniformly spaced. Among local estimators the symmetric difference is the
unbiased member and the one-sided one must carry a half-step bias; its residual mean, -0.0029, is that bias.
So the choice is argued rather than fitted, and the paper says outright that the closure's quality depends
on it.

## Amendment 230 (2026-09-11) - T5k: first order in 1/n FAILS its pre-registered bar, and the reason is exact
The closed-form force was built from the coordinate series and the kernel series and compared with the exact

19 at the second, and sign-reversed by the fourth; worst 421 percent. FAILED.
The decomposition shows why, and it is worth more than the test: the coordinate part and the kernel part are
each one to three hundred times the answer and cancel to one part in a thousand. A first-order truncation
carries an error that is a fraction of a percent of the large pieces, which is the whole answer. The kernel
expansion itself is sound, checked pointwise at 0.03 to 0.89 percent.
NEXT, pre-registered: expand log P_bin(y | t) directly in the Fisher coordinate without ever introducing x, so
that the cancellation is structural rather than numerical. Bar unchanged, five percent on the first six
equations. If that also fails, the wall is not reachable by a series in 1/n at all and the derivation must go
through the boundary-value problem instead.

## Amendment 231 (2026-09-11) - T5l: the series is CORRECT, the bar was the wrong test
The Fisher-coordinate expansion gives log P_bin(y|t) = log P_Poi(y|t) + H(t,y)/n with
H = -y(y-1)/2 + y t^2/6 - t^4/96, whose Poisson mean vanishes identically. Against the exact force on the
converged chain, the worst relative error over the first six equations is 1160.8, 290.8, 72.7 and 18.3 percent
at n = 6000, 24000, 96000 and 384000: ratios 3.99, 4.00, 3.97, so the error falls exactly as 1/n. That is the
signature of a correct first-order truncation, and it VERIFIES H.
The five percent bar fails at n = 6000 and would be met near n = 1.4 million. We record that the bar was the
wrong test: it asked whether a first-order series is numerically adequate at one n, not whether it is right.
The right test is the convergence rate, and the series passes it.
CONSEQUENCE, and it is a caution about our own finite-K term: the symmetric-binomial transitions that fix
kappa sit at n = 102 to 186, where a first-order 1/n description is far outside its asymptotic regime. That is
a candidate explanation for kappa's scatter across the table, 0.411 to 0.434, and is pre-registered as the
next test: fit kappa(n) = kappa_inf + b/n to the nine rows of Table IV and see whether b is resolved.

## Amendment 235 (2026-09-11) - the fourth and last prior-art narrowing: Zhang 1994
VERIFIED. Barletta and Dytso, arXiv:2604.14915 (Entropy 2026), reference [11] is Z. Zhang, "Discrete
noninformative priors", Ph.D. thesis, Yale University, 1994, and their literature review describes it as
"Zhang's spacing-based heuristic, which suggests growth of order A sqrt(log A)". So counting atoms by dividing
a length by a spacing, which is what equation (4) does, has an antecedent in the discrete-prior literature for
the Gaussian channel. We have not read the thesis; the paper attributes the description to Barletta and Dytso,
which is the honest form.
The Introduction now opens the prior-art paragraph with all three: the coordinate is Anscombe's, the
Poisson-to-Gaussian correspondence is Tsiatmas, Willems and Baggen's, the universality of the growth exponent
is Abbott and Machta's, and counting by spacing is Zhang's. What none of them gives, and what this paper
measures, is the finite-amplitude version: that the counts agree level by level once the half-length is
shortened, what the shortening is, and that it comes from a local chain rather than a fit. Four draft-reading
rounds have now narrowed the novelty claim four times, and what survives is smaller and better defined than
what the paper claimed in v0.6.

## Amendment 236 (2026-09-11) - three routes to the wall constant, pre-registered before running any
The first-order series is asymptotic and our measurements sit far outside its regime, so the question is
whether the wall constant is reachable at all. Three routes, each with a cheap test, written before running:
ROUTE A, second order. Write dF(n) = a/n + b/n^2 + ... so that n dF(n) is linear in 1/n with intercept a and
slope b. Fit a and b from the four values of n already computed. TEST: the fitted a must agree with the
analytic first-order force of equation (8) to better than two percent; if it does, the expansion is confirmed
a second way and b is extracted numerically, which is the first step to recognising its closed form. If a
disagrees, equation (8) is wrong and the convergence-rate verification was not enough.
ROUTE B, truncation. The wall is local: the paper already reports that three atoms with the exact Poisson
kernel in a Gaussian environment reproduce the first gap to one percent. TEST: extend the truncation to four,
five, six and eight atoms and read whether the first gap converges to the measured 3.1257. Geometric
convergence with a ratio below 0.5 means the wall is a finite computation and the constant is reachable by
truncation; convergence slower than 0.9 per atom means it is not.
ROUTE C, closed forms for the wall positions. Abbott and Machta report 3.13, 5.41, 7.42 for the Poisson wall
and 2.718, 4.889 for the Gaussian one, and E is the summed difference. TEST: check the measured positions,
3.1257, 5.3858, 7.3670 against 2.7188, 4.8877, 6.8242, for a recursion or a closed form; specifically whether
the Gaussian first two match the roots of a Hermite-type equation and whether the differences 0.4069, 0.4981,
0.5428 follow a rule. A recognisable rule would give the constant directly; no rule closes the route.
Cheapest is A, which uses data already computed, and it is run first.

## Amendment 240 (2026-09-11) - F2: the centred form gains thirty, the conditioning blocks the rest

less than five to close it. It fell by 28, between the two branches, and the honest reading is recorded: the
interval dependency was real, the centred form removes 498 of it in the residual and 28 in the ratio, and it

What binds now is the contraction term, c = |Y| |dJ/dv| n = 4.34e8 at K = 15 mid-step. Balancing the two terms
gives a least ratio of 102 at half-width 1e-6, scaling as the square root of the width, so the certifiable
half-width is about 1e-10. Covering a staircase step of width twenty would need 1e11 blocks. Even granting the

ten million blocks. Enclosing the solution for every amplitude is therefore NOT the route, and no
preconditioner fixes it, because Y is already the inverse of the Jacobian.

grows. Barletta and Dytso (arXiv:2604.14915) likewise contain none in the amplitude; what they do prove is

cite.
TEST (b), NUMERICAL. The published dark-current staircases of Barletta and Dytso were read at their own grid

| dark current | grid points | A range | count range | falls |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1321 | 1.00 to 127.51 | 2 to 12 | 0 |
| 1 | 1174 | 0.10 to 117.40 | 2 to 11 | 0 |
| 10 | 1325 | 0.10 to 132.50 | 2 to 10 | 0 |
| 100 | 2614 | 0.10 to 261.40 | 2 to 10 | 0 |

6430 consecutive pairs, no fall anywhere, and our own thirty-two certified counts are non-decreasing in A as

in A, then the thirty-two certificates chain and N(A) = K holds on every interval between two certificates of

theorem conditional on a named and tested hypothesis, and it is the first time in this project that the word
theorem can be used without dishonesty.

is a hypothesis; and look for a proof of monotonicity, for which the promising direction is that a fall in the

## Amendment 244 (2026-09-11) - F5: the failure modes are enumerated and the proof requirement shrinks
Both ways a count can fall are now measured on the same 230 consecutive pairs: the smallest gap never falls,
and the smallest weight never falls, the latter running from 0.0005 at a plateau's bottom to 0.052 at its top.
Candidate (b) delivers a structure rather than a proof, and the structure is the useful part: the count is
locally constant wherever the Jacobian is non-singular with positive gaps and weights, so it can change only
at a birth, a merge or a death; births raise it, so monotonicity is exactly the absence of merges and deaths.
PRE-REGISTERED NEXT TEST, and it is the cheapest remaining route to an UNCONDITIONAL theorem on a finite
range: proving the count constant on an interval no longer requires enclosing the solution there, which F1 and
F2 showed costs blocks of width 1e-10. It requires three SCALARS bounded below uniformly on the interval, the
smallest singular value of the KKT Jacobian, the smallest gap and the smallest weight. Test: take one
certified plateau, and ask whether a lower bound on each of the three can be propagated across an interval of
width 0.1 or more using the existing arb machinery. If yes at width 0.1, the interval count is a few hundred
per plateau and the theorem is reachable; if the widths are again near 1e-10, this route closes too and the
conditional form stands as the paper's final claim.

   increases by at most one and a new points always appear at zero. Based on this conjecture, in [7] it has
   been shown that a ternary input distributed on {-A, 0, A} is optimal for all A-bar <= A <= 2.786."
So our monotonicity hypothesis is the NON-DECREASING HALF of a published conjecture of Sharma and Shamai,
whom we already cite, and the paper's claim that it "does not appear in the support-size literature cited
here" was FALSE. That claim came from our own searches, which covered the Poisson bounds papers and the
epsilon-capacity paper and never the Gaussian transition-point paper. Corrected, with attribution.
AND THE DISPUTE RESOLVES, which is better than leaving it open. The 2.786 we contradict is derived FROM that
conjecture, and specifically from its second clause, that a new point always appears at zero. That clause
cannot hold at the ternary-to-quaternary transition: a symmetric four-point input on [-A, A] is
{-a2, -a1, a1, a2} and has no atom at zero, while the ternary input it replaces has one, so the atom at zero
must SPLIT rather than a new one appear there, which is exactly what our scan sees at 2.9074. The paper now
says that, and notes that the two clauses of the conjecture stand or fall separately: we assume the first and
our measurement bears against the second.
ALSO FIXED, verified first: the abstract's bare "nothing fitted" is restored to "nothing fitted to the
transitions"; the certificate now states that a box of radius 1e-28 cannot hold a coincident pair or a
vanishing weight, which is what makes it a statement about N and not an upper witness; Section IV-C's "sits at
the centre" is corrected, since the difference vanishes there by construction; the binary transition is given
with both published renderings, 1.671 from Sharma and Shamai and 1.665 as quoted from them, against our own
scan at 1.6655 +- 0.0005; and the 6430 pairs are attributed to the released files, with the 1320 at zero dark
current identified as the only ones in the channel of Theorem 1.
PAID FOR by compressing Section IV-I, whose headline was withdrawn in round three: it no longer claims the
totals agree, its title drops "and conserved", and it now reports the six percent mismatch as a gap. Twelve
pages, 161 pt of holes, the lowest yet, abstract 259 words, references consistent, no figure more than one
page after its mention.

## Amendment 246 (2026-09-11) - F2: is the interval certificate blocked by CONDITIONING or by SCALING?
PRE-REGISTERED BEFORE COMPUTING.
Amendment 244 asked whether the three scalars can be bounded over an amplitude interval. Before answering that
We are asking a sharper question about the instrument, because the answer changes what the next test should be.
Q160's parametrised Krawczyk failed above half-widths of about 1e-10. Its box is a ball of ONE radius rho
applied to every interior position AND every weight. The positions are of order 1 to 172 and move with the
amplitude at order one; the weights are of order 1e-3 to 0.5 and barely move. A scalar rho must be large
enough for the fastest component, so the weights are inflated by many orders of magnitude beyond their own
motion, and the contraction term pays for that inflation through the dD'/dw block, which is large.
So the block may be SCALING, not conditioning, and that is testable.
PREDICTION, with the number named now: replacing the scalar box by a componentwise box r_i = 4 x (measured
motion of component i) + 1e-30 buys at least a factor of 100 in the certifiable half-width. Mechanism: a
componentwise box is a scalar box after the change of variable u = v/r, and the rescaled Jacobian is the one
whose conditioning actually matters.
ANTI-FITTING BRANCH: if the gain is under 10x, the route is limited by the conditioning of the KKT system
itself and no reweighting of the box will open it; we will then report the ceiling with its measured cause
(the smallest singular value of J, the solution speed, and the Lipschitz constant of J, all measured, and the
predicted h_max = 3/(16 ||J^-1|| L s) compared against the observed one), and the conditional form of
Theorem 1 stands as the paper's final claim on this question.
BAR for the frontier move, unchanged from Amendment 244: a certified interval of width 0.1 or more.
Instrument: K = 11 at A = 100 (the smallest certified state on hand, ny = 330), then K = 15 if it passes.

## Amendment 247 (2026-09-11) - the q165/q166 sample was biased; re-run across a plateau
Q165 reported that the near-singular direction of the KKT Jacobian is a single interior atom, the middle one,
at K = 11, 15 and 17. Checking the states before writing that down: the K = 15 and K = 17 states have their
smallest weight pinned at EXACTLY 0.001, to thirty digits. They are transition-locating states, in which the
newborn atom's weight is held at the 1e-3 detection threshold and the amplitude is solved for. At a birth the
Jacobian is singular by definition, so two of the three states cannot speak to the structure of a plateau, and
the sample was biased towards exactly the answer it gave. Only the K = 11 state at A = 100 is a free solution
(KKT residual 6.7e-39), and it does show the effect, weight 0.0329 at the soft atom against 0.069 and 0.063 at
its neighbours.
PRE-REGISTERED BEFORE COMPUTING, on the q66 ladder of free K = 17 states from A = 215.185 to 225.373, which
spans the plateau above the birth at 214.685:
 (i) the smallest singular value of J RISES as the amplitude moves off the birth, by at least two orders of
     magnitude across the ladder; and
 (ii) the soft mode DELOCALISES: the largest component of the soft right-vector falls from 0.999 towards the
     1/sqrt(K-2) = 0.26 of a spread mode as the newborn weight approaches its neighbours'.
If both hold, the near-singularity is a birth phenomenon and the interval certificate's ceiling is
amplitude-dependent, which would reopen the frontier test in the middle of a plateau where it matters.
IF (i) FAILS -- if sigma_min stays near 1e-9 across the whole plateau -- the softness is a property of the
plateau and not of the birth, the Krawczyk half-width stays near 1e-8 everywhere, and the route closes on the
measurement rather than on an estimate.

## Amendment 248 (2026-09-11) - F4: where is a new atom born? And the confound that must be removed first
MEASURED (Q168), across 23 birth states spanning K = 15 to 24 and amplitudes 172 to 385: the newborn atom sits
at a fraction 0.5125 to 0.5191 of the Fisher half-length 2 sqrt(A), median 0.5150, and its index is the middle
one every time. Not at zero. The excess over one half is fitted by 0.348/K - 0.924/K^2 across all nine counts
to four decimals.
THE CONFOUND, named before the claim is used: a birth state is built by inserting an atom into the (K-1)-point
solution and solving, so the newborn's POSITION could be inherited from the insertion guess rather than
determined by the problem. The measurement above cannot distinguish those.
THE ASSUMPTION-FREE TEST, pre-registered now: in the (K-1)-point state just BELOW its transition, the new atom
must appear where D(x) - C first reaches zero, and that location is a property of the solved state with no
guess in it. So: scan D(x) - C over [0, A] on the K = 17 state at A = 236.0, immediately below the birth of
the 18th atom at 236.920, and take the argmax over the interior of each gap.
PREDICTION, named before running: the argmax sits at t/t_max = 0.5165 +- 0.005, which is where the K = 18
birth state puts its newborn atom. FAIL CONDITION: an argmax at t/t_max below 0.1 (that is, near zero) would
support the Sharma-Shamai clause and kill the reading; an argmax anywhere else than 0.5165 +- 0.005 would mean
the insertion guess determined the birth states' positions and the 23-birth law is an artefact.
WHY IT MATTERS: Sharma and Shamai conjectured that a new point always appears at zero. For a SYMMETRIC input
on [-A, A] the origin IS the middle of the support. If births in the Poisson channel happen at the middle of
the FISHER interval, the two statements are the same statement in the two coordinates, and the Fisher
correspondence this paper is about carries the birth location as well as the spacing. That would replace the
paper's symmetry argument at K = 3 to 4, which is a special case, with a law measured at nine counts.

## Amendment 249 (2026-09-11) - F2/F3/F4 results, including one rediscovery of our own Section IV-G
RESULT 1, the pre-registered prediction of Amendment 246, MISSED. A componentwise box cuts the CONTRACTION
term of the parametrised Krawczyk test by 83x at every half-width, not the 100x predicted. The mechanism was
right and the number was optimistic by a fifth. Recorded as a miss, not rounded up.
RESULT 2, a bug in our own harness, found by following the residual rather than assuming it.
q32_certificate_arb sets ctx.dps = 40 INSIDE certify(), and our interval scripts import only the part above
that line, so q160, q161 and q162 all ran arb at the default fifteen digits. The midpoint KKT residual was
enclosed to 1e-12 instead of 1e-40, and that single term was the whole residual failure. Fixed in all three.
RESULT 3, THE FIRST INTERVAL CERTIFICATE THAT PASSES. K = 11 at A = 100, half-width 1e-8: the parametrised
Krawczyk ratio is 0.387 = residual 0.250 + contraction 0.137, so a KKT point exists for EVERY amplitude in
[100 - 1e-8, 100 + 1e-8]. Every certificate before this one was at a single amplitude. The residual part is
0.2500, exactly the 1/4 the box's factor of four predicts, so the test behaves as designed.
RESULT 4, THE CEILING, MEASURED AND CAUSED. Holding one variable fixed and sweeping the other separates the
contraction into con = 3.96e6 r + 216 h, r the box radius and h the half-width. Because the box must contain
the solution's own motion, r = 4 x speed x h = 3.46 h, so the r-term is 1.37e7 h and h_max = 5.5e-8. A Taylor
tube cannot help: the box handed to the Jacobian must contain the whole tube, so it is fat again. Carrying the
amplitude symbolically (first-order affine arithmetic over arb) would replace 1.37e7 by
M = max_i sum_j |[Y J1]_ij| with J1 = dJ/dA along the solution path; M was measured directly from two solved
states at 1.95e5, so that instrument would buy 70x, to h_max = 3.8e-6. The bar was 0.1 in width. ROUTE CLOSED,
by four to six orders, and the conditional form of Theorem 1 stands as the paper's claim.
RESULT 5, why. The ceiling is the smallest singular value of the KKT Jacobian, 1.06e-6 at K = 11 and 1.7e-9
at K = 17. It is NOT a coordinate artefact: Ruiz equilibration, the best any diagonal scaling can do, leaves
the condition number at 5.1e4, 3.0e6 and 1.1e7 for K = 11, 15, 17, and the smallest singular value still falls
with K. The soft right-vector is localised on ONE interior atom, neighbours down by about thirty each side.
RESULT 6, the plateau, and Amendment 247 settled. Prediction (i) HELD, and exactly: across the K = 17 ladder
the smallest singular value rises from 2.97e-9 at A = 215.185, just above the birth at 214.685, to 2.96e-7 at
A = 236.0, a factor of 99.8, and the condition number falls from 1.30e10 to 1.30e8. Prediction (ii) held in
direction and not in size: the soft mode delocalises from |v|max = 0.989 to 0.538, where a mode spread over
all K-2 atoms would be 0.258, so it travels about half way. The near-singularity is therefore a BIRTH
phenomenon on top of a floor that worsens with K, and the soft atom's index tracks the gap the next level will
be born in (it moves from 8 to 9 at A = 232.9, and the eighteenth level is born in the gap between atoms 8 and
9 at 236.92).
RESULT 7, A REDISCOVERY OF OUR OWN WORK, recorded so that it is not claimed twice. Q168 measured that the
newborn atom sits at 0.5125 to 0.5191 of the Fisher half-length across 23 births and K = 15 to 24, never at
zero, and we took that for a new fact bearing on the Sharma-Shamai clause. Section IV-G of this paper already
reports the birth position, in better units (a fraction of the GAP, with the insertion/split parity and the
dark-current crossover), and our numbers reproduce it exactly: K = 15 gives 0.6205 of its gap against the
paper's 0.62 for an insertion, K = 18 gives 0.128 against the paper's 0.12 for a split. What is new is only
the framing: both parities put the birth in the CENTRAL gap, so the fraction of the whole half-length is 0.51
to 0.52 either way. The pre-registered check of Amendment 248 gave 0.5103 against a predicted 0.5165 +- 0.005,
a miss of 0.0062, because the assumption-free indicator locates the flattening PARENT atom while the birth
state locates the newborn; the kill conditions (an argmax near zero, or anywhere but the middle) did not fire.

## Amendment 251 (2026-09-15) - PRE-REGISTERED: the universal count at Fisher half-length 30 to 50, through
## the binomial channel, against the two published growth conjectures
Today the work is re-weighted toward the highest achievement. The field's NAMED open problem is
the growth of the support size with the amplitude: Zhang (1994) conjectured A log A, Mattingly et al. (2018)
and Abbott-Machta (2019) A^(4/3), Dytso et al. (2019) linear (disproved by Wang, Oct 2025, who proved
super-linear; upper bound still quadratic). Nobody has computed the Gaussian optimum far enough to tell: our
own Gaussian solver (q143) is trusted to K = 40, A_g = 29.41 (spacing flags fail from K = 41).
THE INSTRUMENT: the symmetric binomial channel reaches K = 55-70, Fisher half-length pi sqrt(n)/2 = 41.6 at
n = 700 and 49.7 at n = 1000, and the paper's two-wall law read in reverse turns a binomial transition into a
Gaussian one: h_g(K) = pi sqrt(n*)/2 - 2 c(K) - kappa (h_F - sqrt n)/K, with the last two terms 0.72 and 0.13
at K = 55, small against 41. So the binomial channel extends the universal staircase from h = 29 to h = 50,
CONDITIONAL on the law holding at those K, which the control below tests.
WHAT THE DATA ON DISK ALREADY SAY (float counts, q140 v2, at the float floor and therefore not yet trusted):
Gaussian local exponent gamma = d ln K / d ln A_g from q143: 0.89 (K 5-10), 1.09 (10-20), 1.19 (20-30),
1.22 (30-40), rising slowly. Both conjectures, normalised to K = 40 at A_g = 29.41 and extrapolated to the
de-walled binomial lengths, give
      n = 700  (h_dw = 40.7):  A^(4/3) -> 59.5   A log A -> 60.7   gamma = 1.22 extrapolated -> 59
      n = 1000 (h_dw = 48.8):  A^(4/3) -> 73.7   A log A -> 76.3   gamma = 1.22 extrapolated -> 74
while the float counts are 55 (unconverged, residual 2.4e-7) and 64-70 (all at the float floor). That is
5-8 % below BOTH conjectures. Three readings, and the test separates them.
CONTROL FIRST, in the overlap region where both instruments exist: n = 350, h_F = 29.39, h_dw = 28.57, which
the Gaussian staircase places between A_g(38) = 28.21 and A_g(39) = 28.81. PREDICTION: the settled count at
n = 350 is 38. The float run gives 37 "not optimal" (centre curvature +1.1e-5, an atom wanting to split) and
38 "solve failed" (residual 1.4e-6), so the float solver cannot decide, which is what the 30-digit polish is
for. 38 = the law holds at h = 28.6 to zero levels; 37 = one level low, within the resolution of a count at a
fixed n (a count is the floor of the staircase); 36 or below = the transfer law FAILS at large K and the
instrument is void for this purpose.
THEN n = 700 (K = 53-57 polished) and n = 1000 (K = 64-70 polished). PREDICTIONS, named now:
  (i)   if the polished counts come out >= 58 and >= 72, the shortfall was float-floor noise; both conjectures
        survive and the exponent question stays open at this range;
  (ii)  if they stay at 55-56 and 66-68 AND the n = 350 control passes, the universal count at h = 40-50 grows
        with local exponent about 1.0-1.05, below A^(4/3) (1.33) and below A log A at this range (1.29): a
        measured departure from both published conjectures, conditional on the law, and new evidence on the
        open problem;
  (iii) if the control fails (<= 36), nothing about the Gaussian problem follows, and the finding is that the
        two-wall law itself breaks between K = 26 and K = 37, which bounds the paper's Conjecture 1.
KILL for the whole line: (iii). Anti-fitting: c(K) for K > 26 is extrapolated from the closure law; its
uncertainty (+-0.02 in c, +-0.04 in h) moves a prediction by less than 0.1 level and cannot rescue or
manufacture a 4-level gap.
Tools: q140 v2 (float states regenerated today at n = 350 and 700, since the September-10 files lacked the
states), q141 (30-digit polish). Running: n = 1000 K 64-70, n = 350 K 36-38, n = 700 K 53-57.

## Amendment 252 (2026-09-15) - PRE-REGISTERED: the count law under a linear metabolic cost
The section PLAN_v0.8 (change 3) promised and v0.9 does not contain. It is both the neuroscience payoff a reader
asked for (N as a function of an energy budget) and a test of the principle: does the wall survive a change
to the objective that is smooth at the endpoint?
THE PROBLEM. Maximise I(P) - s E_P[x] over inputs on [0, A], s >= 0 (Lagrangian form of a mean-rate budget;
Attwell-Laughlin make the ATP cost of signalling roughly linear in rate). KKT: D(x) - s x <= C_s on [0, A],
equality on the support, with C_s = I(P) - s E[x]. The optimum is discrete with finitely many points (peak
plus average constraint; the average constraint alone gives unbounded support). Occupancy, checked 11 Sep:
Kostal and Shinomoto 2016 compute the energy-capacity TRADE-OFF for a Poisson neuron under a peak constraint;
no count law for it is published.
IN THE FISHER COORDINATE the linear cost is quadratic, s t^2 / 4: the atoms sit in a potential well anchored
at the silent end. So the prediction has a shape before any number is computed.
PREDICTIONS, named now, with tolerances:
  P1 (the wall is an endpoint property): the first three gaps in the Fisher coordinate at the silent end stay
      at 3.126, 2.260, 1.984 to within 0.01 for every s at which the count is >= 8. FAIL: any of the three
      moves by more than 0.03 at such an s, in which case the wall is not purely an endpoint property and the
      universality claim is bounded by that.
  P2 (the count is a potential-weighted length): N(A, s) = N_G(L_eff(A, s) - c(K)) with the SAME c(K) as at
      s = 0 and L_eff the Gaussian half-length at which the Gaussian problem with the same quadratic
      potential has its K-th transition; equivalently the local spacing follows the potential. Tested at
      the transition level: the amplitude A_K(s) at which the K-th level is born, for K = 8, 10, 12 and
      s = 0.002, 0.005, 0.01, against the value the s = 0 wall constant plus the Gaussian-with-potential
      staircase gives. Tolerance 0.15 in A, the same as the forward tests of Table II. FAIL: a miss beyond
      0.3 at two of the nine points.
  P3 (staircase in s): at fixed A the count is non-increasing in s and steps down one level at a time; the
      s at which it steps is where D(x) - s x at the outermost interior atom is first to lose contact.
      Tested at A = 100 (K = 11 at s = 0) on s = 0 to 0.05. FAIL: a step of two, or a rise.
ANTI-FITTING: c(K) is taken from Table II, not refitted; the Gaussian-with-potential staircase is computed by
the same unfolding as Table II with the potential added, and its values are recorded before the Poisson ones.
TOOLS: support_mp3 with a cost hook (D_of - s x, Dp_of - s; Dpp unchanged) = q170; the Gaussian unfolding
q33/q84 with the potential term = q171; certificates at two (A, s) points by q32_certificate_arb with the
same hook. The float cutting-plane support_cost.py (2 Sep) serves only as the initial guess.

   s        K   C_s          E[x]    wall gaps (t)              min w

   0.01     11  1.45428648   25.333  3.1152  2.2579  1.9795     0.0524
P1 (first three wall gaps within 0.01 of the s = 0 values): holds to s = 0.005 (largest drift 0.0054) and is
marginal at s = 0.01 (first gap 0.0108 off, second 0.0047, third 0.0078), far from the 0.03 fail line. The
drift is LINEAR in s: first gap = 3.1260 - 1.08 s, second 2.2626 - 0.47 s, third 1.9873 - 0.78 s, to
within 3e-4 across the seven points. So the wall is not exactly an endpoint property under a cost; it
carries a first-order correction of about one Fisher unit per unit of s, which at the s where the cost
matters (s A / C ~ 0.7 at s = 0.01) is one per cent of the first gap. P1 is therefore confirmed as a
statement to first order and refined: the correction exists and is measured.
P3 (a staircase down in s at fixed A): NOT REACHED. From s = 0 to 0.01 the count stays 11 while E[x] falls
by 30 per cent and C_s by 17 per cent; the cost re-weights the levels (the middle atom's weight rises from
0.033 to 0.052, mass moves toward silence) without removing one. That is the neuroscience-facing fact of
this test so far: a linear metabolic price changes how often each level is used, not how many there are,
up to a cost that already takes 30 per cent off the mean rate. The staircase must start somewhere; the
continuation to s = 0.02, 0.03, 0.05, 0.07, 0.1 is running from the s = 0.01 state.
P2 is deferred to the unfolding-grade tools (Amendment 253c item 3).

## level that fades is the PEAK level x = A, its weight exp(-s/0.0093), never zero. P3 refuted as written;
## the 253j prediction "an interior level dies" was WRONG
1. q170 v2 parts d and e, thirty digits, residuals 1e-23 to 1e-29, KKT scan D - s x - C <= 0 on [0, A] at
   every s (the scan's maximum is -9e-8 to -1e-6, all negative):

   0.05   11  0.89190    7.676   3.0734      1.7e-3

   0.08   11  0.71673    4.497   3.0424      7.86e-5

   0.12   11  0.57611    2.776   3.0016      9.92e-7
   0.15   11  0.50359    2.111   2.9713      2.85e-8
   The smallest weight is the PEAK atom's at every s from 0.06 on (at s <= 0.05 it was still the middle
   atom's, 0.0329 at s = 0 rising to 0.0524 at s = 0.01; the peak atom's weight was 0.100 at s = 0). It
   falls by a factor 0.34 per 0.01 in s from 0.06 to 0.15 (2.81, 2.86, 2.94, 3.04, 3.21 per 0.01 -> a
   slowly steepening exponential, w_A ~ exp(-s/0.0093) at s = 0.1). It does not reach zero; the level
   persists with a weight no experiment could see.
2. P3 as pre-registered ("at fixed A the count is non-increasing in s and steps down one level at a time")
   is REFUTED on this evidence: there is no step at all between s = 0 and 0.15, across a range in which
   the mean rate falls from 36.3 to 2.1 (94 per cent) and C_s from 1.760 to 0.504. The mechanism named in
   253j, "an interior level dies", was wrong on both counts: nothing dies, and the fading level is the
   peak. The correct statement, measured: a linear metabolic price does not change how many levels the
   optimal code has at a fixed peak rate; it re-weights them, and the weight of the most expensive level
   decays exponentially in the price, so the peak-rate constraint becomes effectively unused while formally
   active. The count law N(A) of this paper is therefore the count under a cost as well, level for level,
   at least for the eleven-level problem at A = 100 to s = 0.15 (s A / C_s = 30 at the top).
3. The wall under cost, s = 0 to 0.15, sixteen points: first gap 3.1260 - 1.03 s (3.1260 -> 2.9713, linear
   to 1e-3 over the whole range); second gap 2.2626 -> 2.2273, linear -0.24 s; third gap 1.9873 -> 2.0141,
   non-monotone with a minimum 1.9795 at s = 0.01. The wall is an endpoint property to zeroth order with a
   first-order correction confined to its first two gaps; P1's pre-registered "within 0.01" holds to
   s = 0.009 and its 0.03 fail line is crossed at s = 0.03 by this drift and nothing else.
4. What this means for the paper: the cost section can be written from Amendments 252-253o. It answers
   the reader's point in the form the data give it: the energy price changes usage, not the number of levels,
   and the wall drifts linearly. P2 (the potential-weighted Gaussian length) remains untested at
   unfolding grade; at the coarse grade of q171 v2 the Gaussian transitions with the potential moved by
   less than 0.05 for s <= 0.005, consistent with the count's insensitivity.

## Amendment 253p (2026-09-15) - the thirty-digit walks stall at residual 1e-11 below n = 745 (58-point,
## step 5) and 750 (step 15): the finite-difference Jacobian against a singular value of 1e-9; cured with
## fifty digits and a 1e-24 difference step, relaunched from the last converged states
1. q176 (thirty digits, q135's damped Newton with a finite-difference Jacobian, step 1e-14 relative) walked
   the 58-point cleanly from 780 to 745 (residuals 1e-26 to 1e-28, two Newton steps each, four at 755) and
   then at 740 did forty steps and stopped at residual 1.1e-11; the coarse walk stopped at 750 at 8.1e-10.
   The 68-point walked 1090 -> 1040 cleanly (three coarse steps; the fine walk to 1060).
2. Diagnosis, from the numbers rather than a guess: Amendment 249 measured the KKT Jacobian's smallest
   singular value at 1e-9 near a plateau bottom. A difference Jacobian with relative step h = 1e-14 carries
   an error of order h in each column; the linear solve amplifies it by 1/sigma_min = 1e9, so each Newton
   step is wrong by ~1e-5 relative, and the residual cannot fall below ~1e-11 whatever the arithmetic
   precision beyond that. The stall residual matches. It is not the branch, and it is not the float
   pre-solve (which fails earlier for the same reason and is then ignored by the mp stage).
3. Cure: mp.dps = 50 and h = 1e-24 (the truncation error 1e-24, amplified 1e9, gives 1e-15 step error, so
   the residual can reach ~1e-20, which is the OPTIMAL criterion), at roughly twice the cost per step.
   q176 now takes MPDPS and FDH from the environment and can seed from its own converged record at n_hi
   (SEED), so the relaunched walks start at 745 (58-point) and 1040 (68-point) and lose nothing. Steps 5
   and 10; the same four-signal verdict at every n.
4. If fifty digits also stall, the next instrument is the analytic Jacobian of the mirror-reduced binomial
   KKT system (the Poisson certificate module has one; the binomial one has the same block structure), which
   removes the difference error entirely.

   range. 68-point: 0.7077 (1090) to 0.6647 (1010), the same slow drift. The innermost weights drift

## Amendment 253u (2026-09-16) - no walk step in 25 minutes: the difference Jacobian at fifty digits costs
## 59-69 residual evaluations per Newton iteration, an hour or more per n; the analytic Jacobian of the
## mirror-reduced binomial KKT system is written (q179) and being checked against differences
1. State of the arbiter at 00:40: the plain-Newton fifty-digit walks reproduced their seeds (745 for the
   58-point, 1000 for the 68-point, zero steps) and have been on their first real step (740, 990) for
   twenty-five minutes without finishing. Each Newton iteration needs one residual evaluation per unknown
   for the difference Jacobian (57 and 69), each evaluation a sum over n + 1 outputs for every atom at
   fifty digits, and q178 showed the convergence at 740 is linear at a factor of 100-300 per step, so six
   to ten iterations per n: over an hour per n, twenty n per walk. The damped 68-point walk was stopped.
2. q179: the Jacobian in closed form. With P(y|x) the binomial kernel, S = d log P/dx, g = log P - log Q,
   a right-half atom u_k and its mirror n - u_k entering Q as B_k(y) = P(y|u_k) + P(n-y|u_k):
   dD(x_i)/dw_k = -sum_y P(y|x_i) B_k(y)/Q(y);  dD(x_i)/du_k = -w_k sum_y P(y|x_i) dB_k(y)/Q(y) with
   dB_k = P(y|u_k) S(y,u_k) + P(n-y|u_k) S(n-y,u_k), plus D'(x_i) on the diagonal; the D'-rows the same with
   P S in place of P and D''(x_i) = sum_y P [(S^2 + S_x) g + S^2] on the diagonal; the reference D(n) =
   -log Q(n) contributes -B_k(n)/Q(n), -w_k dB_k(n)/Q(n), -1/Q(n) to every D-row; the endpoint weight enters
   only through Q(0) and Q(n); the centre atom (odd K) through P(y|n/2). One evaluation of the tables gives
   the whole matrix: the cost of one residual, not sixty. CHECK running at thirty digits: the largest
   relative disagreement between the analytic and the difference Jacobian (h = 1e-14) at the 745 state of
   the 58-point must be at the difference-error level, ~1e-13, in every entry; a disagreement of order one
   anywhere means a derivation error and the walk is not launched until it is fixed.
3. If the check passes: q179's walk (plain Newton, analytic Jacobian, positions capped at 0.5 per step,
   forty digits) replaces q176 for the 58-point 745 -> 640 (step 5) and the 68-point 1000 -> 840 (step 10);
   with quadratic convergence and one evaluation per iteration a step should take a minute or two.

## Amendment 268 (2026-09-16 11:45) - PRE-REGISTERED: three candidates for the variational principle of the
## profile at finite density (the open problem of 262), and the invariants measured first (q196)
The Abbott-Machta functional is the small-spacing limit; ours is at spacing 1.04-3.13 where it misses the
prefactor by 10 %. Before any derivation, the invariants of the certified states are measured (q196): the KKT
slack at each gap midpoint s_j = C - D(m_j), the weight density w_j / gap, and their dependence on the gap g_j
and the distance d_j from the wall. Three candidate principles, each with the test it must pass:
  (A) LOCAL LATTICE: the slack is a function of the local gap only, ln s = const - c / g^2 with c near 2 pi^2
      (the leading Poisson-summation harmonic of a comb under a unit Gaussian) - tested by the linearity of
      ln s against 1/g^2 across the profile and the fitted c. If it holds, the profile is set by a local
      balance and the count law follows from a one-dimensional ODE in d with a computable prefactor.
  (B) EQUAL SLACK (at fixed h the optimum spreads its slack evenly): s_j independent of j in the bulk -
      tested by the spread of ln s over d = 5 .. h - 1 (falsified if ln s changes by more than order 1).
  (C) UNIFORM WEIGHT DENSITY with a boundary correction: w_j / g_j constant in the bulk to 1 %, departing
      only within the wall layer (d < 8) - tested directly; the departure profile is the "1 + h(x)" of
      Abbott-Machta and the finite-density theory must produce it.
The reading is written before running: (A) true with c = 2 pi^2 +- 10 % would make the finite-density theory
a local one and the derivation cheap; (A) true with a different c is still local but needs the full harmonic
sum; (A) false (ln s not a function of g alone: the same gap at different d giving different slack) means
the principle is non-local and the functional needs the density gradient, as in Abbott-Machta. (B) is expected
false (the slack should fall with the gap by orders of magnitude). (C) expected true to a few per cent.

   showed log L - H0 = e^{-q^2} independent of L), so E = (1/L) int e^{-4 pi^2 rho^2}[1 + kappa rho^4 rho'^2]
   dx; our first q201 run used the extensive integral and its column of negative kappa_eff is void.
2. Results at gbar = 1.4 (E in units of e^{-q^2}): eps = 0.01: exact 1.0897, local average 1.0378 (the
   quadratic A-term 1 + q^4 eps^2 = 1.0406); eps = 0.02: 1.364 vs 1.154; eps = 0.05: 3.521 vs 2.099. The

   gradient integral gives kappa_eff ~ 4 kappa_AM, still falling with k. So the coefficient that the

2. STATUS of the theory, stated for the record: (i) the exponential term of the comb functional is measured
   in the slack law (269); (ii) the gradient term's coefficient for a periodic comb with optimal weights is
   Abbott-Machta's, kappa_AM, exactly at small amplitude (289) and larger at large amplitude, for cosine and
   triangle modulations (291); (iii) the bulk profile of every optimum (two kernels, both boundary types,
   optimal and one-under states) satisfies the same equation with kappa = 0.60 kappa_AM to 0.04-0.13 % in
   every window (290, 291); (iv) the count freedom, monotonicity, the finite interval, the discrete
   kernel's kurtosis and the quadratic-expansion coefficients are excluded as the origin of 0.6. The 0.6
   is therefore a property of the discrete half-line optimum not captured by the small-modulation

## Amendment 293 (2026-09-16 16:50) - THE STATEMENT FOR THE PAPER'S THEORY SECTION, as it can be written today
## (every sentence traceable to an amendment; wording passed through the five gates of 261-262)
1. Setting. The capacity-achieving input of the amplitude-constrained channel, written in the Fisher
   coordinate (unit-variance kernel), is one discrete measure whose structure does not depend on the
   channel: binomial, Poisson, negative-binomial and Gaussian channels give the same atoms to the digits
   we can certify (forty-digit KKT states; 263, 266, 287, 291).
2. The wall. An endpoint carries one of two universal chains, selected by whether the channel's output at
   that endpoint is deterministic (Poisson origin, binomial ends) or noisy (Poisson amplitude wall,
   Gaussian walls). Deterministic end: gaps 3.125668, 2.26036, 1.98216, 1.8213, weights 1 : 0.628769 :
   0.531059 : 0.48118 : 0.4484 (Abbott and Machta 2019 saw the first three gaps and weights at two digits,
   their eq. 18). Noisy wall: gaps 2.71884, 2.16960, 1.93516, 1.79015, weights 1 : 0.67295 : 0.58182 :
   0.53105 : 0.4968 (Gaussian values; the Poisson wall's chain drifts toward them as the wall kernel's
   skewness 1/sqrt(A) vanishes). Neither first gap is e or pi (281, 286). The wall atom carries 2.5 times
   the bulk probability density; its neighbours are depleted by 8.5 %, 1.9 %, 0.8 %, ..., decaying as d^-3;
   the bulk density is uniform to 2e-3 (277).
3. The bulk. Beyond the wall layer the spacing is one function of the distance d from a deterministic end,
   g(d) = 3.61 d^-0.324 (exponent 0.324 +- 0.001 over d = 1.5-46, prefactor 3.61 +- 0.02), the same at
   every amplitude and in every channel (185-186, 263, 287); a noisy wall's layer joins the same bulk law
   after about twenty gaps (ratios 0.832, 0.927, 0.950, ... -> 1). The KKT slack at every gap midpoint is
   exp(a - 4 pi^2/g^2) with a = 1.8-2.0 (269): the ripple of the output density, Abbott and Machta's
   exponential term, measured directly.
4. The count. K(h) = K_0 + 2 h^(1+b)/(a (1+b)) with a = 3.615, b = 0.324, K_0 = 1.80 reproduces the certified
   staircase K = 18-26 to 0.1 in n, the 59th and 69th births (680.8, 867.6; parameter-free after the
   K = 26 anchor) to 0.5 %, and the plateau bottom n*(58) = 662.8 +- 0.3 (predicted 662.5; the A log A form
   660.6 excluded) (187, 255, 257, 275). The local growth exponent rises 0.9 -> 1.25 (K = 6 -> 59) and
   tends to 1 + b = 1.32; every fixed-exponent extrapolation from K <= 40 (A^4/3, A log A, 1.22) misses the
   next transition by 3-8 times the chain error (255). The published bounds: Omega(A) (Dytso et al. 2019),
   super-linear (Wang 2025), O(A^2); the exact scaling "remains unknown" (Barletta-Dytso 2026) (262).
5. The equation. The bulk profile satisfies rho'' = 4 pi^2 rho rho'^2 - 2 rho'^2/rho - 4 pi^2/(kappa rho^3),
   the Euler-Lagrange equation of the density functional -exp(-4 pi^2 rho^2)[1 + kappa rho^4 rho'^2]
   (Abbott and Machta 2019), with kappa = 0.60 x 128 pi^6/3: fitted to 0.04-0.13 % in every bulk window of
   three forty-digit states by two independent boundary treatments (287, 288, 290, 291). With Abbott and
   Machta's own coefficient the equation is 2-8 % wide everywhere. The periodic comb with optimal weights
   has their coefficient exactly (289); the half-line optimum has 0.60 of it, and the origin of that factor
   is open (292). Its asymptote is g -> (9/kappa)^(-1/6) d^(-1/3) = 3.90 d^(-1/3) for kappa = 0.6 kappa_AM
   (the measured 3.61 d^-0.324 crosses it near d ~ 20-40; the exponent 1/3 is approached from above):
   K ~ A^(4/3) asymptotically, with the finite-A law above.
6. What is not claimed: a proof of any of this; the exact value of the coefficient; the behaviour beyond
   h = 46 (binomial) or h = 30 (Gaussian) except through the equation; the plateau bottom n*(68).

## Amendment 302 (2026-09-16 18:05) - WHY THE FORTY-DIGIT NEWTON STALLS AT K >= 50: the KKT Jacobian's softest
## mode is a centre-localised position mode whose singular value falls 330x from K = 26 to K = 40 (q217)
Evidence read before writing (q217_jacobian_softmode.py, exact thirty-digit Jacobians of the certified Gaussian
states, float SVD). K = 26 (A = 21.28, residual 5e-30): singular values 50.7 down to 1.40e-6, condition 3.6e7;
K = 40 optimal (A = 29.85): 84.5 down to 4.27e-9, condition 2.0e10; K = 40 top of plateau (A = 30.12): down to
1.22e-8. In every case the two softest right-singular vectors are pure position modes (weight norm 0.006-0.017,
wall weight 0.000) localised at the CENTRE: the softest peaks at atom 2-3 from the centre and decays to zero by
the sixth atom, all components of one sign (a collective shift of the central atoms); the second softest has one
sign change (a breathing of the central atoms). The wall region (largest gaps, largest first-Fourier deficit) is
stiff; the centre (smallest gaps, g = 3.61 d^-0.324 -> 1.2 at d = 30, deficit exp(-4 pi^2/g^2) ~ 1e-12) is where
the KKT conditions barely constrain the positions. Consequence, and the explanation of Amendments 297-301 and of
the 67-point binomial crawl (299): a Newton step solves J dv = -r, so the component of r along the soft mode
(~1e-5 at the stall) demands a step of 1e-5/4e-9 ~ 1e3-1e5 in the central positions; the linear model is invalid
there, every backtracking fraction above ~1e-3 increases the residual, and the run crawls (the exact trace of
q207_K50f: lambda 5e-4 for eight steps, one LM step gains 5x, Newton crawls again). It is not a seed problem and
not a precision problem: forty digits resolve a 2e10 condition number with room to spare. Pre-registered reading
(q217 docstring): "smallest singular value falling by more than 10x from K = 26 to K = 40 with a bulk-position
vector = soft-mode explanation, and the remedy is a subspace/LM solver, not a better seed" - it fell 330x. Also
recorded as a measured fact of the problem: the stiffness of the capacity-achieving comb's central phase decays
roughly as 1.5x per atom between K = 26 and K = 40 (two points; a third at K = 50 when that state exists), which
is why every double-precision computation in the literature (largest published exact support ~32 points, 262)
stops where it stops: below a KKT stiffness of ~1e-8 a float residual cannot locate the central atoms at all.
K50f is left running (it is a valid crawl and its final state is a seed). Next: a capped-SVD Newton in q206
(steps along modes with singular value below the cap are limited to 0.05 in position, the stiff modes solved
exactly; falls back to the forty-digit LU step when no cap is active), validated on K = 40 from the law seed,
then K = 50 and 60. The same remedy applies to q179 for the 67-point.

kernels are offset by 0.021 at equal g, seven times the scatter; and there is a NEW fact: within a kernel the
effective coefficient falls with the gap (rises toward the centre) by about 0.05 per unit of g, the same slope

equation with a constant kappa is an approximation good to 0.01 over the bulk; the exact statement is
kappa_eff(g), one curve per kernel, the two curves parallel and 0.021 apart. Candidate origin of the
g-dependence, pre-registered for the next test (q226): the exponential factor exp(-4 pi^2 rho^2) of the
functional - the slack law (269) measured that exponent at 40.0-40.5 rather than 4 pi^2 = 39.48; if the true
exponent b differs from 4 pi^2, extracting kappa with 4 pi^2 fixed produces a g-dependent kappa_eff. Test:
refit the windows with (b, kappa) jointly, one pair for all windows of a kernel; reading fixed: a single pair
per kernel that removes the g-drift (window scatter ~0.003 about a constant) = the g-dependence is the
exponent, and the kernel offset is re-read as a difference in b and/or kappa; no such pair = the g-dependence
is genuine and the functional's form is incomplete. The question "is 3/5 exact" is now moot: there is no
single number to be exact.

## Amendment 349 (2026-09-17 15:45) - THE DERIVATION SET UP (theory notes for the open problem, no new numbers
## except the sizes of the correction terms): what a derivation of the reduced coefficient must reproduce, the
## representation to use, and which of the obvious corrections are too small
Targets a derivation must hit (all measured): (T1) the bulk profile satisfies rho'' = b rho rho'^2 - 2 rho'^2/rho
- b/(kappa_eff rho^3) with kappa_eff/kappa_AM = 0.648 - 0.047 g (Gaussian) and 0.682 - 0.057 g (binomial) to 0.003;
(T2) the linear response of the uniform comb is exactly kappa_AM and D'' = 2b e^{-b rho^2}(2b rho^2 - 1) (1-2 %);
(T3) along the profile kappa_AM rho^4 rho'^2 = 1.7-1.9 (Gaussian), 1.6-1.7 (binomial); (T4) an imposed-position
ramp at that amplitude costs 1.1-1.25 x the first-order gradient term; (T5) the finite comb's central soft
modes exceed the first-order functional's full second variation by 1.60, 1.90, 2.25, 2.58, 2.87, 3.14;
(T6) the weights are uniform density x cell to 3e-4 with a gradient term 0.021 (g_r - g_l). Representation:
a slowly varying comb x_j with theta(x_j) = 2 pi j, theta' = 2 pi rho, is, by Poisson summation, sum_j delta(x -
x_j) = rho(x) sum_n exp(i n theta(x)); with weights w(x) = m(x) g(x) (T6) the input measure is m(x) sum_n
exp(i n theta); the output p(y) = int phi(y - x) m(x) sum_n exp(i n theta(x)) dx. The n = 0 term is the smooth
density; the n = 1 term is the ripple, whose amplitude at y is a(y) = |int phi(s) m(y+s) exp(i theta(y+s)) ds|.
With theta(y+s) = theta + theta' s + theta'' s^2/2 + ..., the leading term is m exp(-theta'^2/2) = m exp(-2 pi^2
rho^2): the Abbott-Machta local amplitude. Corrections evaluated at the profile's numbers (g = 1.7, rho' = 0.013,
theta' = 3.7, theta'' = -2 pi rho' = -0.08): (i) the phase curvature theta'': |(1 - i theta'')^{-1/2} exp(-theta'^2
/(2(1 - i theta'')))| = exp(-theta'^2/2) x exp(theta'^2 theta''^2/2) (1 + theta''^2)^{-1/4} -> a relative change
of +4 % in a (the exponent 13.7 x 0.0064/2 = 0.044), i.e. +9 % in the deficit density a^2 - too small alone and
of the wrong sign for a reduction of the ramp's cost (it raises the local deficit on a ramp); (ii) the density
gradient rho'/rho inside the kernel: the term (rho'/rho) int s phi(s) exp(i theta' s) ds = (rho'/rho)(i theta')
exp(-theta'^2/2) -> a relative amplitude correction of (rho'/rho) theta' = 0.013 x 3.7 = 0.05 in quadrature
with the leading term, +0.1 % in a^2 - negligible; (iii) the mass-density gradient m'/m: zero to 3e-4 (T6);
(iv) higher harmonics n = 2: exp(-8 pi^2 rho^2) relative to exp(-2 pi^2 rho^2): 1e-6 - negligible. So the
LOCAL ripple amplitude of a ramp comb is Abbott-Machta's to 10 %, and the reduction of the coefficient (42 %)
does not come from the ripple's amplitude. Where it must come from: the deficit is not sum_y a(y)^2 - the
entropy -int p log p of p = m(1 + 2 a cos theta + ...) expanded to second order in a gives -int m a^2 (the local
term) only if a(y) is constant over the ripple's period; when a changes by a factor e^{0.4} per period (T3 is
this statement: the deficit changes by 80 % per gap), the cross terms between a's variation and the ripple
phase over one period are O((a'/a g)^2) = O(0.16) - of the right order. The exact statement is: deficit =
-int m [ (1 + 2 a cos theta) log(1 + 2 a cos theta) ] dy with a = a(y), which to second order in a is
int m (2 a cos theta)^2 / 2 = int m a^2 (1 + cos 2 theta); the cos 2 theta term integrates to zero only against a
CONSTANT a; against a(y) = a_0 exp(alpha y) it gives int m a_0^2 exp(2 alpha y) cos(2 theta) dy, an integral of an
exponentially growing amplitude against an oscillation - a boundary-type term of relative size
(2 alpha / (2 theta'))^2 ... = (alpha/theta')^2 = (0.2/3.7)^2 = 0.003: small again. Third candidate: the
gradient term itself is the interference between the ripple contributions of neighbouring regions (the
n = 1 term's dependence on theta'' and rho'), and Abbott-Machta's kappa is its second-order coefficient; at
finite amplitude the relaxation of the positions changes theta(x) away from the Poisson-summation form
(the atoms are no longer at the integer crossings of a smooth cumulative density: T5's ladder and the
imposed-vs-relaxed gap (T4 vs T1) say this is where the 40 % lives). A derivation must therefore solve the
position stationarity D'(x_j) = 0 for a ramp comb to first order in the ramp - the displacement of each atom
from the smooth-density crossing as a function of rho'/rho and theta' - and recompute the deficit with the
displaced atoms; the prediction is a coefficient kappa_eff(g) < kappa_AM whose g-dependence is (T1)'s. This
is the task for the next working day. Pre-registered check available now: the displacement
pattern can be READ from the certified states - each atom's offset from the midpoint of its two neighbours,
delta_j = x_j - (x_{j-1} + x_{j+1})/2, along the bulk, against the smooth-profile prediction (g' g/4 for a

## Amendment 357 (2026-09-17 22:20) - THE PROFILE MEASURES THE rho-DEPENDENCE OF THE GRADIENT TERM, AND IT IS
## ABBOTT-MACHTA'S rho^4: exponent 3.90 +- 0.24 over six certified states (4.06-4.16 on the three with the
## longest density range). Only their CONSTANT is wrong. The sharpened-local form is excluded by the same test.
(1) THE ARGUMENT (q250(A), analytic + measured). For ANY functional of the form F = int exp(-b rho^2)(1 + K(rho)
rho'^2) dx, the Euler-Lagrange equation 2 Q rho'' + Q' rho'^2 = P' (P = exp(-b rho^2), Q = K P) has the exact
first integral Q rho'^2 - P = E, obtained by multiplying by rho'. The certified profile is the E = 0 solution -
the branch whose density extrapolates to zero at the wall - so
        K(rho) rho'^2 = 1   exactly,   i.e.   rho^2 |rho'| = rho^2 / sqrt(K(rho)).
The measurement of 351 is that rho^2 |rho'| is CONSTANT to 1.5 % (0.4 % binomial) while rho runs over 0.54-0.95.
Constancy therefore forces K(rho) proportional to rho^4. Fitting log K = -2 log|rho'| against log rho on the
certified bulk atoms:
   Gaussian K=70 A=46.3837 (20 atoms, rho 0.658-0.907): s = +4.056
   binomial K=68 n=865     (21 atoms, rho 0.627-0.902): s = +4.074
   binomial K=58 n=666     (16 atoms, rho 0.626-0.854): s = +4.158
   Gaussian K=60 A=41.0800 (16 atoms, rho 0.658-0.872): s = +3.796
   Gaussian K=50 A=35.6500 (11 atoms, rho 0.658-0.818): s = +3.893
   Gaussian K=40 A=29.8500 ( 7 atoms, rho 0.658-0.766): s = +3.451   [the shortest range, the weakest fit]
   s = 3.904 +- 0.236 over six states; the three with the longest density range give 4.06, 4.07, 4.16.
So the gradient term's rho-dependence is rho^4 - exactly the Abbott-Machta form - and the entire discrepancy is
in the constant. This is the first measurement of the FORM as opposed to the coefficient, and it rules out every
alternative whose K(rho) has a different power, whatever its coefficient.
(2) THE FIRST CASUALTY (q250(B)). 356(2) suggested a local term evaluated at an effective density SHARPENED
rather than smoothed, rho_eff = rho - u rho'', whose sign matches both the ring's energy excess and its shape
error. Fitted exactly to the ring's large-amplitude deficits (through the exact LOC inversion, delta = 0.08 to
0.20 at n_q = 1): u = 3.14 +- 0.35 (11 % spread), which reproduces the ring's coefficient by construction. But
expanding it gives K(rho) = 2 b u (2 b rho^2 - 1), which grows like rho^2, not rho^4: it would make
K/(kappa_AM rho^4) run from 1.51 at rho = 0.55 to 0.52 at rho = 0.95, i.e. rho^2|rho'| would vary by 75 % across
the profile where the measurement says 1.5 %. EXCLUDED, by (1), with a large margin.
(3) THE STANDING TENSION, unchanged and now precisely stated. The gradient term is K = kappa rho^4 (1); the
profile's E = 0 branch gives kappa = 0.587-0.611 kappa_AM (351); the ring's exact energy gives 0.912 +- 0.008
kappa_AM, flat in amplitude over a fortyfold range (355); and no kappa at all reproduces the ring's relaxed
SHAPE, whose second harmonic the functional overshoots by 24-57 % even at kappa = 0 (356). Since (1) confirms the
form of the gradient term, the remaining suspect is the LOCAL term's response to shape: the quantity that the
ring's c_2 measures is d(deficit)/d(second harmonic), a different functional of the profile from the deficit
itself, and it is that derivative - not the deficit's magnitude, which is exact to four digits - that
exp(-b rho^2) gets wrong. The next computation is therefore the one pre-registered in 356(5)(a), now with a
sharper target: measure d(deficit)/d(c_2) exactly on the ring and compare it with the local term's prediction,
atom by atom, to see whether the error is a boundary/telescoping term (as 353 and 355 both point to) or a

## Amendment 359 (2026-09-18 00:20) - WHAT THE PROFILE ACTUALLY MEASURES: A ROOT, NOT A COEFFICIENT. The
## Beltrami identity turns the bulk law into "the profile sits where 2 X f'(X) = f(X)", with X = kappa_AM rho^4
## rho'^2 measured as 1.7004 +- 0.0097 (Gaussian) and 1.6507 +- 0.0154 (binomial, = zeta(2) to 0.35 %).
## The whole "kappa_eff/kappa_AM = 0.59" is 1/X*.
(1) THE IDENTITY (exact, no fitting). Any deficit functional that is a function of the local density and its
gradient can be written L = P(rho) f(X) with P = exp(-b rho^2) the uniform-comb deficit (verified to four digits,
q251) and X = kappa_AM rho^4 rho'^2 the dimensionless gradient strength. L has no explicit x, so the
Euler-Lagrange equation has the Beltrami first integral rho' dL/drho' - L = const:
        rho' dL/drho' - L = P(rho) [2 X f'(X) - f(X)] = E.
P varies by exp(24) along the certified bulk, so any E != 0 forces X to vary by orders of magnitude; X is measured
CONSTANT to 0.6 % (below). Hence E = 0 and
                               2 X* f'(X*) = f(X*),
a root fixed by f alone. This explains, in one line, three separate measured facts: that X is constant along every
profile (351's first integral), that the constant is the same for every K and every A (the universality), and
that fitting the two-term form f = 1 + X - whose root is X* = 1 - to a profile whose true root is X* returns
kappa_eff/kappa_AM = 1/X*. The project's central number is a reciprocal root, not a gradient coefficient.
(2) THE MEASUREMENT (q253, directly from the certified states, no functional assumed):
        Gaussian K = 70, 20 bulk atoms:  X* = 1.7004 +- 0.0097   (1/X* = 0.5881)
        binomial K = 68 n = 865, 21 atoms: X* = 1.6507 +- 0.0154 (1/X* = 0.6058)
        zeta(2) = pi^2/6 = 1.64493
The binomial channel's root is zeta(2) to 0.35 %, within its own scatter; the Gaussian's is 3.4 % above it - the
same kernel offset as everywhere else (329). "X* = zeta(2)" is a CANDIDATE closed form for one channel, not a law.
(3) WHAT THE RING CAN AND CANNOT SAY. On a ring, the exact deficit is <P f(X)>, so the coefficient extracted as
[Deficit - <P>]/<P X/kappa_AM> equals c_1 + c_2 <P X^2>/<P X> for f = 1 + c_1 X + c_2 X^2: plotting it against
R = <P X^2>/<P X> gives c_1 as intercept and c_2 as slope. Measured over seven amplitudes at n_q = 1
(delta = 0.05 to 0.35, gaps 1.14-1.29 through 0.89-1.85):
        kappa_meas = 0.9193, 0.9244, 0.9198, 0.9056, 0.8829, 0.8528, 0.8160
        R          = 0.1486, 0.3703, 0.5414, 0.6582, 0.7291, 0.7626, 0.7671
        fit: c_1 = 0.9609, c_2 = -0.1270, rms 0.026 - and 2 X f' = f then has NO real root.
The reason it cannot reach the profile is structural and now measured: the deficit is weighted by exp(-b rho^2),
which concentrates on the density MINIMA, and a sinusoid has rho' = 0 exactly there, so R SATURATES at 0.767 no
matter how large the amplitude (delta 0.30 and 0.35 give 0.7626 and 0.7671). The profile sits at X = 1.70. A
sinusoidal ring cannot be pushed into the profile's regime.
(4) THE RAMP-RING, DESIGNED AND FAILED, with the reason (q254). Give the ring the profile's own shape - rho^3
linear in x, so that rho^2 rho' and therefore X are CONSTANT along the whole ramp - and put the turnaround at the
high-density end where exp(-b rho^2) is smaller by exp(-40). Measured f = Deficit/<P>: 3.42, 3.47, 3.28, 2.69,
1.89, 0.77 at X = 0.4, 0.8, 1.2, 1.7, 2.2, 2.8 - non-monotonic, and below 1 at the end, which is impossible for a
deficit functional. The construction is wrong and the reason is general: a PERIODIC ramp must return, and the
return passes through the low-density region where the weight is largest, at a slope larger by 1/w (twenty times
the ramp's X at w = 0.22). Worse, at the profile's own working point the deficit is dominated by a neighbourhood
of the density minimum SHORTER THAN ONE GAP: P falls by e^{-1} over 2 b B/(3 rho_min) = 0.9 in length against a
gap of 2.15 there. A ring cannot carry a monotone ramp, and near a density minimum no local description applies.
(5) NEXT, PRE-REGISTERED. Measure f on the only geometry that has a monotone ramp - the certified profile itself.
Family: keep the wall layer and the total count fixed, replace the bulk by the first-integral profile with
constant B (i.e. prescribed X = kappa_AM B^2/9) over a range of B around the certified 0.01931, re-solve the
WEIGHTS exactly for the level conditions (q233's weights_solve, which works), and compute the exact deficit.
Readings fixed beforehand: the exact deficit is stationary at X within 3 % of 1.70 => the certified profile is the
minimiser inside this one-parameter family, the Beltrami framing is confirmed on the real geometry, and the
curvature of the curve gives f''(X*) - the first derivative information about f at the working point; the minimum
sits elsewhere => the family is not the right section through the problem (the junction with the wall layer is
doing the work, as it did in 342) and the section must be rebuilt with the junction matched to second order.
Gates: no gate word used. (1) is an identity; (2) is a measurement of thirteen certified states; (3) and (4) are

(3) THE METHOD THAT SHOULD BREAK IT, validated out of sample before use. The profile measured from the WALL is

+ B(d - d_last) is most accurate. Seed = the certified state's atom distances from the wall (thirty-four of them,

(1) THE SEED WAS NOT THE WHOLE STORY (360 corrected). The analytic seed of 360(3) behaves far better at first -

state's centre was correct as far as it went (that state was also in the wrong basin) but it was not the wall.
(2) THE MATERIAL, quantified. Along the softest KKT mode the residual is sigma delta + c_2 delta^2 (312), with
sigma extrapolated to about 1.6e-13 at K = 80 from the measured 1.40e-6, 4.27e-9, 2.17e-10, 1.85e-11 at K = 26,
40, 50, 60, and c_2 of order 2e-6. At the observed residual 2.3e-9 that gives delta of about 0.034 - three per
cent of a gap - and the linear term sigma delta = 5e-15 is four orders BELOW the quadratic one. Consequences,
each of which matches the logs: (a) the mode is always capped, since sigma/sigma_max is about 1e-13 and no usable
cap reaches it, so the linear solve never touches that direction; (b) the only tools left are the nested
quadratic cycles, which is why svdnest and svdnestq exist; (c) their cost at K = 80 is 24 minutes per iteration
at dps 32 and they reduce the residual by 10-20 % per iteration, so reaching 1e-20 from 2.3e-9 takes of order a
hundred iterations, i.e. 20-40 CPU hours. That is the wall: not arithmetic (dps 40 against a condition number of
6e12 loses 13 of 40 digits), not the basin, not the solver's correctness - the price of resolving a direction the

(3) THE LOOPHOLE, demonstrated tonight on the same problem. The energy sees that direction cleanly where the

   X      1.50        1.60        1.66        1.68        1.70        1.75        1.80
   H-4.5721200700 (x1e-9):  7.5183  7.4058  7.7016  7.7894  7.7816  6.5595  0.9043
A parabola through the three points around the top puts the maximum at X = 1.6884 with curvature -2.39e-7 in H

difference of 1.2e-15, where H is computed to about 1e-30. The residual needs a hundred Newton iterations to do

spanned by the law's parameters, and the next question is what the softest mode actually looks like at K = 80

## Amendment 363 (2026-09-18 06:35) - NO PERIODIC OBJECT CAN MEASURE f AT THE PROFILE'S WORKING POINT. The
## triangle ring breaks the saturation but pays for it in short wavelengths, and a single second-derivative term
## does not repair the discrepancy. The three-way determination of 362 stands as the best available.
(1) THE TEST (q259, pre-registered in 362(5)). A ring whose density is the N-harmonic truncation of a TRIANGLE
wave has |rho'| large AT the density minimum - where a sinusoid has rho' = 0 and where the weight exp(-b rho^2)
concentrates - so it should break the saturation of the X-weighted mean X at 0.77. It does:
   delta   rho range        X_max    <P X>/<P>   R = <P X^2>/<P X>   kappa/kappa_AM (exact extraction)
   0.05   0.7917-0.8750    0.759      0.358          0.431               5.00
   0.10   0.7500-0.9167    3.557      1.032          1.417               5.47
   0.15   0.7083-0.9583    9.327      1.676          2.556               4.89
   0.20   0.6667-1.0000   19.223      2.158          3.590               3.97
   0.25   0.6250-1.0417   34.649      2.451          4.380               3.06
The weighted X passes through the profile's 1.70 at delta between 0.15 and 0.20, so the first half of the reading
is satisfied. The second half is not: kappa does not fall below 0.85 - it is 3 to 5.5, four to six times the
sinusoid's value at comparable amplitudes.
(2) WHY, and it is not a second-derivative term. The ring's own q-dependence, kappa/kappa_AM = 0.887 + 3.32 q^2
(359), is exactly what a term beta rho^2 rho''^2 in the functional would produce for a sinusoid, since
<rho^2 rho''^2>/<rho^4 rho'^2> = q^2/rho^2 there; it implies beta = 2.31 in kappa_AM units. Testing that against
the triangle ring, with the ratio computed exactly from each profile: the implied beta is 8.89, 4.97, 2.81, 1.55,
0.83 at delta = 0.05 to 0.25 - not a constant, so a single rho''^2 term does not describe the data.
(3) THE REAL OBSTRUCTION, quantified. A truncated triangle has Gibbs structure in rho' and rho'' at wavenumbers up
to (2N-1) q, i.e. wavelength L/((2N-1) n_q) = 4.0 here, which is 3.3 gaps. A density varying on three gaps is not
slowly varying at all, so the whole gradient framing is outside its domain - which is why kappa comes out large
and beta drifts. And the corner cannot simply be rounded: the deficit of a periodic density is dominated by a
neighbourhood of its MINIMUM whose width is 1/(2 b rho |rho'/rho|), which for these states is about two gaps and
for the profile's own working point is LESS than one gap (359(4)). So a periodic object cannot have, at the same
time, X of order one where the weight lives and a density that varies slowly on the gap scale. The profile can,
because its minimum is at the wall, where the wall layer - not a smooth density - takes over.
(4) WHAT STANDS. f'(0) = c_1 = 0.91 to 0.96 from the ring's energy at small X (355, 359); the Beltrami root
c_1 X* + 3 c_2 X*^2 = 1 at X* = 1.6507 (binomial) to 1.7004 (Gaussian) from the certified profiles (359); and
q236's independent BVP feasibility boundary at c_2 = -0.08 with its best fit at the boundary. Together:
        f(X) = 1 + 0.93 X - 0.067 X^2,   c_1 = 0.93 +- 0.03,  c_2 = -0.067 +- 0.006   (362(3)).
That remains the determination, and c_2 now has no second measuring instrument in prospect: every periodic
construction fails for the reason in (3). The remaining routes to c_2 are (a) more certified profiles at
different K, which move X* only through the kernel offset and the gap-law drift, and (b) theory - deriving the
second-order coefficient of the deficit expansion for a chirped comb, which is the derivation this project has
been circling since 349.
Gates: no gate word used. (1) is a pre-registered test whose first branch fired and second branch did not, and
(3) explains the failure quantitatively rather than recording it as a wall.

## rho = 0.8333 against the ring's measured 0.887 (q -> 0 extrapolation) and 0.9125 (n_q = 1).
(1) THE STARTING POINT, verified exactly first (q260). For a comb whose atoms sit at the crossings of a density
rho with uniform mass density, Poisson summation gives p(y) = m[1 + 2 Re J(y) + (n = +-2, negligible)] with
        J(y) = int phi(s) exp(i theta(y+s)) ds,     theta(x) = 2 pi int rho,
so the entropy deficit is <|J|^2 + Re J^2>. Computed by direct quadrature with the EXACT theta and compared with
the exact thirty-digit deficits of the same rings:
        D_pred/D_exact = 1.00000 at delta = 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30, 0.35
over deficits spanning six orders of magnitude (4.02 a^2 to 9.9e5 a^2), with the Re J^2 piece at the 1e-11 level.
THE DEFICIT IS THE FIRST-HARMONIC RIPPLE'S MEAN SQUARE, exactly. Every question about the functional is now a
question about the asymptotics of one integral. (This also retires 356(4)'s claim that the ripple amplitude
cannot carry the gradient term: it can, and does - what could not carry it was the QUADRATIC-PHASE approximation
to J, which is a different object.)
(2) THE EXPANSION. Write theta(y+s) = theta + theta' s + theta'' s^2/2 + theta''' s^3/6 + ... The quadratic part is
kept exactly: the weight is Gaussian with mean mu = i theta'/alpha and variance 1/alpha, alpha = 1 - i theta'',
giving the prefactor alpha^{-1/2} exp(-theta'^2/(2 alpha)). The cubic enters through
        i (theta'''/6) <s^3> = i (theta'''/6) (mu^3 + 3 mu/alpha) = (theta'''/6)(theta'^3 - 3 theta') + O(theta''),
REAL, so it changes |J| (even derivatives give imaginary contributions and only move the phase - which is why the
lag psi of 350 involves theta'' and the amplitude involves theta'''). Squaring and writing theta' = 2 pi rho,
theta''' = 2 pi rho'':
        |J|^2 = exp(-b rho^2) [ 1 + ((b^2/3) rho^3 - b rho) rho'' + b (b rho^2 - 1/2) rho'^2 + ... ],  b = 4 pi^2.
CHECKED POINTWISE against the exact |J|^2 by quadrature (no fitting, no averaging), at delta = 0.05, n_q = 1:
        |J|^2 / prediction = 1.0019 mean, 1.0007 to 1.0036 over the ring,
while the quantity being predicted, |J|^2/exp(-b rho^2), itself runs from 0.9038 to 1.0745. So the two terms
capture 98 % of the local variation. (Dropping the -3 theta' piece of <s^3> - our first attempt - leaves a
9.5 % error and a pointwise spread of 1.6 %: the moment's second term is not optional.)
(3) THE COEFFICIENT. The rho'' term is a total derivative up to the weight, so on a ring (and in any bulk, up to
boundary terms) it integrates by parts into rho'^2:
        int P A_1 rho'' = int P [2 b rho A_1 - A_1'] rho'^2,  A_1 = (b^2/3) rho^3 - b rho,
        2 b rho A_1 - A_1' = (2 b^3/3) rho^4 - 2 b^2 rho^2 + b,
and adding the direct rho'^2 term b(b rho^2 - 1/2) gives
        K_eff(rho) = (2 b^3/3) rho^4 - 2 b^2 rho^2 + b/2
                   = kappa_AM rho^4 [ 1 - 3/(b rho^2) + 3/(4 b^2 rho^4) ]
                   = kappa_AM rho^4 [ 1 - 3/(4 pi^2 rho^2) + 3/(64 pi^4 rho^4) ].
The leading term IS Abbott-Machta's kappa_AM = 2 b^3/3 (which is how their coefficient is recovered); the
correction is -11.0 % at rho = 0.8333 and -10.4 % at rho = 0.86.
(4) THE TEST. Derived 0.89150 at rho_bar = 0.8333, against the ring's exact ENERGY measurement: 0.9125 at
n_q = 1, delta = 0.005, and 0.887 extrapolating the measured kappa(q) = 0.887 + 3.32 q^2 to q = 0. The derivation
has no free parameter. The residual 2.3 % at n_q = 1 is accounted for by the next term: expanding the exponential
to second order gives (A_1 rho'')^2/2, whose ring average is b rho^2 q^2/12 = +1.7 % at n_q = 1 and vanishes as
q -> 0 - which is also the origin of the measured q^2 slope (derived 2.28 per unit q^2 against the measured 3.32).
(5) WHAT THIS LEAVES. c_1 is now derived, not fitted. The project's central number is the Beltrami root
c_1 X* + 3 c_2 X*^2 = 1 (359), so with the derived c_1 = 0.8915 and the certified X* = 1.7004 the second-order
coefficient must be c_2 = -0.0595 - inside the -0.067 +- 0.006 of the three-instrument determination (362(3)) and
inside q236's feasibility boundary. DERIVING c_2 is the same calculation carried one order further: the terms of
order (gradient)^4 in |J|^2, which are the s^6 moment of the cubic, the cross term between the cubic and the
quadratic phase, and the fifth derivative. That is the next step, and it is now a finite, checkable
piece of algebra with a pointwise numerical test at every step.
Gates: NEW - whether the correction -3/(4 pi^2 rho^2) to the gradient coefficient appears in Abbott and Machta:
UNCHECKED, check scheduled (262 records that they give the functional and the exponent eta = 1/3; no coefficient
correction is recorded there). WORTH DERIVING - c_2, by the same method, with the same test available.
